div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS

DON'T ridicule the poor man who supports ten Or a dozen dogs. Perhaps that's the only way he has to keep pup. HE was fond of singing revival hymns, and his wife named the baby Fort, so that he would want to hold it. As old maxim says—" A straw shows which way the wind blows." A loose-fitting straw hat is not a bad indicator, either. ENFANT Taaraßik.—" And did they go into the ark two by two?" Mamma—" Yes, dearest." Enfant Terrible---" Well, who went with auntie?" Two women were detected smuggling tobacco in their bustles. Why should not a woman have a tobacco bustle as well as a bustle to back her? LIVE within your income, says the practical ad- viser; but if he would tell how one may live with- out it he would have the merit and the glory of instructing a larger constituency. "DID you hear about the burglar who was arrested this morning 2" " No. What for 2" "For breaking into song." "Is that so 2" "Yes; he'd got through two bars, when some one hit him with a stave." A SCOT, being shown Niagara, was asked if he had ever seen aught so beautiful and strange. He replied: " Weel, for bonny, I'll no say, but eb,mon, for queer, I ance saw a peacock wi' a wooden leg -at Peebles." AN orator who was in great demand in political campaigns, being asked by an admirer the secret of his success, replied—" When I have facts, I give 'ern_ facts; but when I haven't I yell and saw the

air." A CERTAIN caravan orator at a fair, after a long yarn descriptive of what was to be seen inside, wound up by saying—" Step in, gentlemen; step In I Take my word for it, you will be highly delighted when you come out." "MIKE, why don't you fire at those ducks, boy I Don't you see you have got the whole flock befo)l your gun ?" "I know I have; but when I get good aim at one, two or three others will swim right ur betwixt it and me." _ _

_ Visfrou (at the almshouses)—" Poor man I suppose you never learned a trade or profession?' Pauper—" I used to be a waiter." "In a private family?" "No ; at a hotel." "My goodness What did you do with your wealth?" SWIFT'S Stella, in her last illness, being visited by her physician, he said—" Madam, I hope we shall soor get you up the hill again." " Ah," said she, "I air afraid before I get to the top of the hill I shall be out of breath."

BLANCHE—" Have you made any conquests thil summer ? " Lilian—" Oh, yes; Mr. Jones proposec the day before we came away!" Blanche—" Doesn't he pop the question in the most awkard mannei imaginable?" 'they meet now as strangers. A SCIENTIFIC CHAP, who has counted them declares that one-half of the adult men of America
are bald-headed. Yet at least three-fourths art

married. This proves that one-fourth of the met are happy. If it doesn't prove that, what does it prove? " TELL that man to take care of his hat in Court,' -said a judge the other morning to an officer. The offender, who turned out to be a lady, wearing s fashionable sailor hat, indigantly exclaimed, "I an ,no man, sir I" Then said his konour, "I am Jae judge." EDITOR: "You say you wish this poem to appeat in my paper anonymously?" Would-be contributor '" Yes; I don't want any name to it." "Why not?' -"Because lam conscientious about this matter. l ,don't want an unjust suspicion to fall upon some innocent person." •Miss AUGUSTA MAYNE (to Pat Chogue, who hat just tendered her his seat)—" You have my sincere -thanks, sir I" Pat Cheque: "Not at all, mum; not at all. It's a duty we owe to the sect. Some iolks only does it phen a lass be pretty, but I mays zaps I, 'The sect, Pat,' says I, 'not the indivi dool l"

A CURIOUS post-card was received by a firm it Cincinnati some time ago. It was from a custome3 infthe mountains of Tennessee, and read as follows —"please send me side of bacon a bbl of flour l‘ lbs. of coffee and a wheelbarrow my wife had r baby last week and a monkey wrench crops is mid. Mins TRAvis—" Oh, Mr. Meeter, I want to ter you how much 'enjoyed that beautiful little triplet of yours in the Inland Magazine I" Mr. Meetet -(blushing)—" You mean triolet, don't you, Mist Travis?" Miss Travis (blushing furiously)—" Oh -yea! I beg your pardon." Sioz..LADY (to Bridget, with cazds)—"Didn't I Instruct you to say, Bridget, to any one that calle that I ,was too ill to be seen ?" Bridget—" Yis shure,rmurn, I forgot hit intirely. an' oh, mum, the) do have such beautiful dresses on." Sick lad) (rousing herself)—" You may say to the ladies Bridget, that I will be down at once." Yoma ,WEITER (to friend)—"Did you read my story in the Every Other Weekly, Fred, entitled "A Night of Horror ?" Friend—" I read a little of It last evening, Charley, but I worked very hard yesterday, and just as I reached the part where the demon seizes her with both arms and plunges intr ak bottomless abyss. I fell asleep." INTERS.VING QUESTION.—At a debating clut the question was discussed whether there is more happiness•in the possession or pursuit of an object. 'Mr. President," said an orator, "suppose I was courtin' &fel and she was to run away, and I was to run after her, wouldn't I be happier when I eotch'd her than when I was running after?" A GENTLEZIAN was dining lately at one of our fashionable ,hctels. Early peas bad just come in season, and ,every body called for peas, peas, until, they were alLgone. The gentleman was very fond of peas, but Le was too late; so, rising and throw- ing himself into the attitude of Patrick Henry, he exclaimed: "cGentlemen may cry peas, peas, but there is no peasr Ax American was journeying in a railway car- riage with an English lady and her little boy, when the latter produced a cocoanut, and, with a juvenile faith in the resources of the affable stranger, asked him for a hammer with which to break the shell.

" No, sonny," was the Yankee's reply, "I've no „ hammer; but fli tell you what. We're going to stop at a station ,directly, and then I'll buy you a sandwich. It'll do better than any hammer, you •bet 1"

Gisinums," faltered•the young man, "I despair of being able to exptess my feelings toward you as I would like, and lam afraid you will not have the patience to listen to me. I—l always was kind of slow and tunglesome, you know." "Shadrach," said the maiden softly, but with a perceptible business-like ring in har voice, "if you think you can express yourself in 15 ininates I will listen to you. I expect Mr. Epoonamore at nine o'clock." And the young man was just L 6 seconds by the watch in expressing himself. Poor unfortunate Mr. Spoona- more I When be came, he wakentertained by Miss • Ginevra's good old motter. A Puzzrarrt.—A bootblack at. a hotel brought a a traveller one morning a pair, of boots, the leg of one of which was much longer than the other. "How comes it, you rascal, that these boots are not .of the spr.,..e length?" he exclaimed. "I really do not know, sir; but what bothers me the most is that the pair down stairs are Ap , the same fix," re- plied the bootblack.

A tfANbeing overtaken by a shower, sought • shelter from,the rain im the house of a negro fiddler. On entering, he found the negro in the only dry „spot in the htuse—the chimney corner—as happy .s a clam, Addling almost merrily. Our traveller tried to keep. dry, but the rain came in from all quarters. "Jack," said he, "why don't you dx your house?" -..1), cause 'er rain, sol.can't." ,atut wily don't you ftn it when it don't rain "0, when 'er don't rain 'er ti:.n't need no fixing."

TICIEMICOLLECMOR, in making his collection, Inds an old gentleman fumbling in his pockets for his ticket. Ticket collector —" Tickets, please!" Old gentleman— "fm just lookiu' for it:" Ticket- look in again in a fewminutes; see and have it ready eSen." Ticket-collector returns shortly, but the old gectleman is still hunting for it. ficket.collector, suddenly—" Why, you have it in 'tour mouth, man 1" Old gentleman, giving him the ticket—" Oh, so j hae I Here you are I" Another gentleman in.tbe carriage, as the train moves on, to first gentlematt—" I'm .afraid you're losing your memory, sir!" First gentleman—" Nae fear o' that! nae fear o' that. The ticket was a fortnight auld, ,uld I was just bitin' the date aff't I" Tableau! YOUNG TWELES (faint-hearted: "Just think, angel mine, how poor I am. Why, what could I snake of you r She (bravely): "Well, you could make Mrs. Tifjdes of me it you have any nerve." ONE ot our young athletes, whose tongue is developed even more than the rest of his body, was expatiating to a young lady friend, whom he had honoured by a call, on his ability as a walker, the other evening, at 11.30 p.m., and was told by the sweet girl that she would dearly love to see him walk.

AT the court of Queen Elizabeth, Sir Walter Raleigh was one day askin-, a favour of the queen, when she said: "Raleigh,' when will you cease to be a beggar ?" "When your majesty leaves off bestowing favours," he replied.

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

Golf is all the rage now, and even the doctors are infatuated. Instead of sending their patients to Continental watering places they say, "Go to St. Andrews, and play golf." Sir Charles Russell has just been despatched to the capital of Golfland by his medical adviser.

Mr. Steenstrand, the "cotton king,". who failed on Tuesday, is about fifty-five years of age. Up to 1883, when Morris Ranger failed, Mr. Steenstrand was little. if at all, known in connection with cot- ton, and his association with the business has been for the most part, if not exclusively, speculative.

Mr. Gladstone is busy with his books. Many of them will always have an exceptional value from his habit of making notes on the tly-leaves, gene- rally at the end of the volume, as to the page on which he has found any very useful or remarkable passage. He speaks, it is said, of his intention to be in London at the beginning of the -Session, in November.

Mr. Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish-American, who is now staving at Cluny Castle, Perthshire, has a fine houseful of men who light and lead. Amongst them are the lion. H. H. Fowler, Sir Walter Foster, Mr. John Morley, Mr. Cardow, Mr. Yates Thompson (proprietor of the "Pall Mall 'Gazette"), and Mr. Mcßride, sculptor. The latter has executed some commissions for the Iron King, and has orders for more.

One of the leading delegates of the Trade Union Congress is Mr. W. J. Davies. of Birmingham. Mr. Davies has not been a delegate for some years now. He used to be Mr. Chamberlain's great organiser amongst the working men of Birmingham. Mr. Chamberlain rewarded him by making him a fac- tory inspecior. Mr. Davies xecently threw up the inspectorship and returned to his trade as a brass- worker. This was not welcome news for Mr. Cham- berlain.

"Looking Backwards," says a correspondent, "is having a great sale in South Australia. The book- sellers say some thousands of copies have been sold. It materially leavens the public mind in favour of co-operative life as distinguished from the system of competition. The Manchester doctrine that human labor is a mere commodity is ceasing to be believed by the bulk of the people. Books like Looking Backwards' are pushing on this immense change of view concerning human labor."

The dukedom has not made his Grace of Manches- ter a bit prouder. In spite of all temptations to belong to other stations, he remains still "Uncle Kim." An infant elephant sucking a babyzs feed- ing bottle is on show at Belfast. and one evening the duke, accompanied by a party of friends, including Dick Dunn, the bookmaker, visited this elevating entertainment. His Grace consented to name the animal. A table was brought into the ring, with bottles of champagne ;vomit, and the .elephant was christened "Dick Dunn's Irish Stowaway.

The town of Sedan, from which twenty years ago the smoke clouds of battle had hardly passed away, has been so changed by removal of the forti- fications that the German 'victors would hardly know it again. Then it was surrounded by walls now the site of those walls is occupied by. buildings and gardens. To recall the great proceedings of which this week is the anniversary one must visit the cottage on the Douchery read where the Emper- or Napoleon and Count Bismarck transacted the business of surrender, which is arranged as a sort of Sedan museum.

When Colonel North went to Chili he engaged Dr. Russell the " Times " war correspondent, as historiographer with the salary of an ambassador, and he has got a small beer chronicle in return. Dr. Russell," who allowed himself and his profession to be degraded by becoming the salaried appanage of a millionaire has;' says the " Rialto," ." proved how incompatible such a T.losition is with literature. Dr. Russell was Colonel North's man, and so he had to submit to the ostracism of the Chilians, thus losing the best sources of material for a good book, and had to attend his patron at so many jollifi- cations that he had to do his sight-seeing ,by proxy."

Mr. Michael Davitt is in the Strand at work on the "Labour World," which is to see the light ,on the 20th of September. Mr. Davitt will maintain that the workers are entitled to the fruits of their toil, and the nation to the enjoyment of its land. Trades unionism and co-operation, will, of course, figure prominently in his columns. The editor will leave it to others to decide whether he is driving at Socialism, or the co-operative commonwealth, or some other ideal condition, and to label his methods accordingly. Peasonally, he is satisfied to be iden- tified with the labour movement, and to take his stand there. The paper will be a Home Rule organ, independent of Mr. Parnell, Mr. Gladstone, and everyone else. Mr. Davitt is in excellent spirits over its prospects.

The Bishop of one of the Lancashire sees tells a good story, and he has generally to " trot it out" on social occasions when two or three of his chief assistants are gathered together. It is about a Methodist local preacher whom his lordship once heard holding forth to a crowd of open-mouthed hearers in a Yorkshire village. The preacher was drawing a moral from the story of the Prodigal Son, and was adding force to it by a vivid sketch of the joyful return which followed the misery of the out- cast. " I can see him myself at this moment," he shouted, gathering inspiration from his enthusiasm. " There is the home he has deserted, and there on the threshold stands the father he has left. A happy welcome awaits him, and his misery will soon be at an end."

" The marks of his degrading occupation are on him yet. Cannot you see him? There," pointing with his finger into space, "There he is, now, Up to his eyes i' pig muck. ."' This was carrying realism a little too far for the Bishop. He had to leave hur- riedly, and bottled up his laughter till he turned the corner.

Mr. Broadhurst is closing his career as a trade union official with great vigour. He has found in twenty years of leadership among working-men that Liberalism and the progress of his class are practically synonymous. He knows that, in spite of loud professions of standing between the two great parties, others will arrive at the same conclu- sion. He has held a political office in which Lord Rosebery and the Speaker were among his prede- cessors. If his speech occasionally lacks refinement, it is never wanting in clearness and shrewdness. In resigning his salaried office Mr. Broadhurst does not.intend to abandon his position as a Parliament- aryleader of workmen. If his health permits, it is, I am told, his intention to offer himself for re-elec- tiondn'Nottingham, and he has let the cottage he has built for himself at Cromer, where he proposes to live only in the seasons when it is unlet and he is not engaged in London.

Every Liberal will welcome Mr. Arthur Bentley's appearance , in the field as the candidate for Bury in opposition to bir Henry James, or perhaps, we ought to say, the James plus Derby interest. Mr. Bentley is the leader of the Liberal party in Bury, and he has already distinguished himself by his captaincy of the campaign against the drainage schemestfor.theibenent of Lord Derby's property, to which Lord Derby will not contribute one farthing. Under his guidance, the agitation against our ini- quitous system of local taxation has been taken up by the whole town of Bury irrespective of party, other Lancashire towns joining in. Mr. Bentley's election ought to be .sure, for Bury is well organis- ed. Judging by Sir Henry James's speech it has already had the .effect of waking alp the Tory- Unionist member. Mr. Bentley is the proprietor of the revivified "Bury Times "and a large contractor. His face, at once shrewd and kindly, is .adorned by lgold spectacles. The President of the Trade Union Congress, Wm. Matkin, was born on .sth June, 1845, at kaythorpe, Lincolnshire. He was educated at the ,Chtirch Natioual School, and later for two years at aprivate school. He is a carpenter and joiner, and worked for some year' in Westminster. Mr. Matkin repre- sents the Trade Council of Liverpool and the vicinity. An elder brother of his, Charles, is also a delegate to the Congress. He was born in 1845, and represents; the London district of the General Union of Carpen- ters and Joiners. The father of both was William Matkin, village car' enter. His address was aston- ishingly advanced, and its advanced nature in no wise seemed to frighten the great army of delegates. Mr. Matkin is of tne sturdy order of build, with grizzled beard and square head. An ideal ehairman he may not be. But then, who is? But he is very clear-headed upon general principles, and even if the Congress more than once got out of hand the fault was physical rather than metaphysical,

Mr. Bradlaugh communicates through his weekly organ very confidentially with his friends. The last number begins—'On the whole I have got through the long session better than I expect Pd." It continues—"l have only ventured on one course of lectures, that at Manchester, and have chiefly tried to earn my living by signed magazine and news- paper articles." In another part he says, " When this reaches the reader I hope to be on Loch Long fishing. I shall remain with the fishes and the midges until midday Saturday, 13th September, re- turning to London by the night mail. Although I have not worked this year nearly so hard as in the thirty-five previous years of ray life, I have felt less able than heretofore to bear any heavy strain, and I need the rest I take." I heard a good story • con- cerning Mr. Bradlaugh to-day. At one of his con- tested elections at Northampton, when the Tories had their best hopes of success, his opponent asked for his autograph, and in re/Ay Mr. Bradlaugh wrote :—" House of Commons.—Admit Mr.--to the strangers' gallery," and followed this with his signature.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6 1890 An when they unlapt th' handikchsr to won SAWT ! ! ! Nob'ry could mek it eawt, thad wer th' beauty o' Smith's trick's (nobbut his name worn'd Smith), an' Smith's mate med ackeawnt o' being as gloppen'd as onybody.—From "The Blackburn Standard and Weekly Express."

div.head: WEEK AT BLACKPOOL.
div.p: A WEEK AT BLACKPOOL.
BY TITNI 0' DICK 0' BOB'S

Mestur Editor,—Aw think aw tn-w-d tha as aw wer thinkin' o' gooin' deavvn to th' owd spot for a tooathri days? Well, aw've bin, an' come back ageean, wonst moor an' wonst less, an' aw've awter'd mi opinion o' Blackpool a goodish bit sin aw wer theer this time; aw've fun eawt as familiarity does breed contempt, becos when aw lived theer fo,r seven year, aw ne'er keered owt abeawt th' place so far as thinkin' id bonny went. Aw'd bin readin' o'er a bit o' verse bi an owd Blackpool writer co'd Joe Baron t' other week, i' th' form ov a invitashun —but aw'll copy id eawt for tha

:AN INVITATION TO THE BRIGHTON OF THE NORTH. Pray come down to Blackpool this summer, But don't think it such a " come down : " Come down when each verdant new corner By the natives and Sol is "done brown." 'Comedown, and your spirits ?twill lighten, Come down, and drain Pleasure's deep cup; palm down to our fair Northern Brighton, And you'll find it will brighten you up. If you come down to Blackpool in (W(h)it week We'll pepper you well with our jokes; And you'll say that not one is a bit weak, For weak witin Whit-week's a hoax. For our Peers we have piers that are peerless To destroy one would be a disgrace, For the town would look empty and cheerless Although a pier less wat'ring place. We have Inns for the folks who are outing, Where hail fellows quaff Hollands gin ; ' We have houses for those who stand doubting, Where visitors are "taken in." Come down, if it's hailing we'll hail you ; Come down, if it's raining you must; Come down, and you'll find we assail you, When you "come down with plenty of "dust."

.Ther's a gret deeal to be said agean Blackpool, an' I ther's a gret deeal to be said for id • for instance yo'll hear a lot o' fooak co' id a dear shop, a ginger- bread sooart o' place, a this. thad an' Vother hoyle, —owt bid enuff. But i' spite o' this, aw challenge , onybody to menshun a nicer, handier, chepper,moor enjoyable place to spend a tooathri days at nor Blackpool is for Lankysher fooak ; yo' see these Yorksha watterin'-places, sich as Scarbro', hes to draw on th' eeast wind for ther seea breeze, but ,deawn at Blackpool yo' ged 'em fro' th' west—and plenty on 'em too. An' at th' Yorksha watterin'- places yo' heyn'd so much choice iv yo're fond o' sailin' as yo' hey at Blackpool. When aw wer deawn at Scarboro' aw could nobbut see booats for Whitby alf-Sawtburn-bi-th'-Seea, an' th' sail to booath on ' 'em wer clooase to th' shoore o' t' way, to say nowt o' t' big cherge for gooin'. Aw know o' no place nobbut Llandudno as hes a bit o' choice that road, an' even theer it's nowt to Blackpool, for at eazar •watterin'-place yo' con tek yo'r choice between Llandudno an' th' Isle o' Man for three bob, or Barrow, for Porness Abbey ruins, an' Morecambe for a bob less; Seawthpooart can be sailed to for abeawt fifteenpence, an' yo've abeawt feour heawrs an' a hofe theer. An' wheer else con yo' ged sich a good tanner's wo'th as yo' con at Blackpool Winter • Gerdens, th' Royal Perk Gerdens, Ohmy's Circus, an' th' 'Quarium ? Or sich a good two-pennoth as th' North Pier an' concert in a mornin', an' a three mile ride on th' Lecktrick tram ? Then look at th' Bathin'. (N.B. Aw wish th' Teawn Clerk o' Black- pool wod get a bye-law med fooarcin' bathers to goon th' watter till they ged aboon th' ankles ; it's disgraceful th' way some bathers carry on.) But aw wer tellin' tha abeawt goin' theer, an heaw bracin' it wor. Aw sailed to Barrow, an' aw med wod they co' a pun; tha sees aw wer thad hongry wi' sailin' aw wer thinkin' a lot moor about eytin' nor th' musician' on board, an' when a chap as wer wi' me said, "lie's givin' us a Selection o' Welsh airs." aw said, "Ay, an' aw wisht he'd give us a selection o' Welsh rapput." Nod so bad, eh ? Forness Abbey's a bonny spot—it's poem i' stooan, but dorn'd thee gooa too near some o'th stooans or else tha'll see wheer o' sooarts o' gaurc- less leatherheyds hes bin an' gooan an' cut ther names; th' fooak as looks after th' place owt to catch 'em at id, an' then nick 'em listen to thi' guide till he runs o'er th' history o' th' place a , dozen times beawt stoppiti. Thad'll cure 'era! But Blackpool's terble short o' musicianers an' quacks, for aw ceawnted 'em misel, an' tha may rely o' wod aw say beein' true when aw tell tha as they dudn'd average moor norfive hunderd different uns a day wheer aw stopt ; thad wer abeawt three hunderd yards seawth a, th' Seawth Pier, sooa 'appen they'd reych a theawsand different uns a day i' th' busy perts. Id wor lively at times when we geet competition at th' front o' th' lodgin's, an' th' best bit o' fun as aw see wer when a brass band (three players) lickt a teeam o' eight niggers i' less nor two minutes; id were rare gam, aw'll assure tha. Tek my advice, fooak, an' when yo've hofe-a- day an hofe-a-creawn to spend, or a bit moor time an' a bit moor brass, spend 'em at Blackpool, an' , yo'll nod rue id. Jus t hevin' menshun'd Blackpool, hesbethowt me ov a bit o' gam a Blegburn chap hed at Blackpool, an' wod he won by hi; but aw'll tell yo' th' tale as aw heeard id an' then. MnsrEn SMITH (though that isn'd th' graelely name) were oloz th' life an' sowl ov a company, an' this bit ov a mattock as he bed wer when he wer deawn at Blackpool, an iv' he could but ha' repeated th' performance at another shop he'd just abeawt , ha' cleared his " exest But to my sheeps. Him an' another mate wer in a pub one afternoon hevin' a glass, an' ther wer a good tooathri fooak th' same reawm doin' ditto; o' at wonst this Smith (as awn co' him) put his glass deawn wi' a bang, an' when ev'rybody sterted lookin' at him he put his hand on his jaw-booan, poo'd his face, an' grooaned. " Wot's up ?" said one gentlemon ; " tooth- wereh

said th' gent. y,a s 't' ysatihd i ng to Smith. oi a ye," "Id is," said Smith, " but there is one good thing abeawt id, an' thad is there's a simple an' certain cure as teks id away in a jiffy." "An' wod is thad ?" a tooathri on 'em axt. " Sawt," said Smith. " Sawt "they axt. Ay, sawt; yo'll see in a minute," an' Smith rung th' bell, an' when th' waiter coom he towd him to bring a handfull o' sawt in. When th' waiter went for id Smith (thad wern'd his gradely name, think on) give 'em o' quite a leckter on wod a grand thing sawt wor, tellin"em heaw useful id wor for catchin' brids bi puttin' id on ther tails, and a lot moor beside; an' when th waiter browt th' handfull o' sawt, he med id up into a parcel in his hankicher an' took id to th' tire to werm. Then he said: " Thad'll be warm enuff for me to put on when aw come back in a minute or two;" an' he went eawt o' th' reawm. This mate ov his then said to th' company, " Wodn'd id be a bit o' gam to hey yon chap a bit ov a leg lip? Let's empty his sawt eawt ov his hankicher an' put some ass in, an' then see heaw id acts. Aw dorn'd believe a word abeawt sawt bein' sich a good thing." Sooa they o' said varra weel to this,an' th' mate wer th' mon to do wod he'd propoosed, an' he'd nobbut just nicely finished when Smith coom th' reawm, felt at th' sawt (?) an' sayin' " It's just reet," popt id to his cheek. Good lorjus ! heaw thad company dud try to keep fro' laffin' when Smith crackt o' wod a grand thing sawt wor—he could feel id dooin' him good o' ready; he knew th' feel o' sawt ony- time, an' through owt. Smith's mate seemed to relish id moor not onybody, to judge hi th' way he winkt at o' th' place; at last one on 'em could howd no longer, soots, he brast off wi' : " Arta sure that's sawt thi handkicher e I "To be sure," said Smith. Aw dar bet the a bob an' a drink as id isn'd," said th' chap. "Done," said Smith. " An' awil bet th' same," said Smith's mate. "Done ageeati." said Smith; "does onybody else want to loyse a bob an' a drink ?" Soots to mek a long stoory short they ev'y one bet him, an ther wet o'er twent); on em.

div.head: r , : NEW BOOKS, &c..
div.p: r , : NEW BOOKS, &c..

"The Handy Book for Invalids," is the title' of a work on dietary in the treatment of disease, by Dr. 11. S. Pardon. There is a large amount of informa- tion in this little work, which is valuable to people in health as well as invalids, for it contains a con- siderable number of recipes and statistics, showing the relative worth of various classes of food. Dr. Purdon, in his introductory remarks, says :—"ln the following pages it will be observed that I have dis- carded all kinds of fish, flesh, and fowl, with alcoho- lic beverages, from my dietary." There will be some .readers who will wonder what can be left to them, but who will find on consulting the work that there is plenty to 'go at,' even when these things have been 'knocked off.' The publisher is Mr. C. W. 011ey, of Belfast._ _. •

From the same firm we have "A Short History of the Church of Ireland," by the Rev. L. A. Pooler, M.A. This work is given merely as an introduction to the study of larger and more important works on the subject, but it is due to the writer to say that he has briefly condensed a by no means small number of larger works, and has brought a vast amount of matter into a comparatively small space.

'A Plunge into Space" is the title of a new novel by Mr. Robert Croinie, who some time ago wrote an excel- lent story called "For England's Sake." The present story is on wholly different lines. It gives an account of a supposed visit to the planet Mars, vgith details of their mode of travelling, and what they saw in this new world. The characters introduced are, on the whole, clearly drawn, and the descriptions are throughout admirable, without in any case being tedious. There is a good deal of quiet humour and satire scattered throughout the novel, which is an altogether interesting and readable one. is published, with a strikingcover, by Messrs. F. Warne' ind Co.—price 2s.

. --- Another novel from the same publishers is from the pen of Mr. J. S. Borlase, and bears the title of " For true love's sake." Mr. Borlase has had a large experience in the art of writing stories for the public, and is careful to have something interesting for every chapter. He is a good hand at" piling up the agony," and manages, there- fore, to keep the reader interested from beginning to end.

" The Encore Reciter," price Is., published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., is a capital selection of pieces in prose and verse, suitable alike for platform purpeses and fireside reading. The completion is made by W. F. E. Marshall Steele ; the selections are from the most eminent authors; and it is a great merit of the publica- tion that two-thirds of the selections have not previously appeared in any similar collection of readings. "St. Maur of the —th," is published by Mr. John Hey- wood, and written by "Quentin Murray," the pseu- donym, if we mistake not, of the author of " Battleton Rectory." But this novel is by no means so interesting as the first work, which was founded in the main upon fact, and close personal experience. There is not much in the way of plot in the novel before us, and, as there is little, either, in the way of moral, the puzzle is why it was written at all.

Mr. Heywood also publishes an analysis of the cate- chism of the Church of England, with examination ques- tions generally intended for candidates, preparatory for the Oxford and Cambridge local, and the College ot Pre- ceptors' examination. It is prepared by the Rev. Lewis Hughes, 8.A., curate of Walcott, Bath, who is the author of various works of the same class on the old and the new Testament. It is obvious throughout that the utmost pains have been taken by the writer to explain in the fullest manner everything that relates to the church catechism, scriptural proof being given in abundance. A revised edition has reached us of "The picturesque guide to Wales," the official publication of the Cambrian Railway Company. The work is edited by Mr. God- frey Turner, who is admirably qualified for the task. We have before had occasion to speak in terms of high praise of this excellent guide, with its wealth of illustrations. The new edition, which is published at 6d., contains ad- ditional views and descriptions of the Mid-Wales portion of the Cambrian line. _

" Bridges "is the title of an interesting little work by Mr. J. W. Rundall, B.A. Ic gives,as might be expected, a full account of Forth Bridge,and shorter accounts of other noted bridges in the world, with explanatory views and drawings. It is published by Messrs. R. and R. Clark, of Edinburgh. We have also to hand from Messrs. Kegan, Paul, and Co., " Cattle Ships," being the fifth chapter of Samuel Plimsoll's second appeal for our seamen ; and "The Tourist's guide to Eastham and the Manchester Ship Canal," published by Mr. George Moores, of Manchester, at the price of 2d.

div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

EAWR CHILDER. When th' owd sun sinks o'er t' distant hills, An' darkness creeps o'er t' sky; An' t' brids sing eawt wi' t' toil o' t' day, As to ther nests they fly; Then, wearied eawt wi' t' toil o' t' day, An, glad for t' welcome rest; Wi' leetsome heart aw mek mi way, To thoose 'at luv me best. Aw know ther's somebry lookhe eawt, Fro' th' oppen cottage dooar ; Aw know ther's anxious een on t' strain, To see mi face once mooar. An' when, at last, .aw ged seet. Wod happy faces shine! As t' childer run to welcome me, An' cheer this heart o' mine. Aw feel repaid a theawsand For wad aw've done throo t' day ; To hear ther merry voices seawnd, An' see 'em o so gay. An' when aw've getten set i' t' cheear, An' reawnd mi knees they cling ; No care nor trouble do aw fear, Aw'm happier nor a king! Ther prattlin' music rings throo t' place, While t' wife sits lookire on Wi' sich a smile, 'at couldn'd fail To comfort th' heart o' mon ! Eawr Kate and Bob 'II tell sich tales- - .

They've allus summa-t new; An' Dick 'll show me o his sums He's lied to do at t' skoo. When t' table's set, an' t' cups are filled, 0 t' chatterin' then 'll cease; NVi' every cheear to t' table drawn, We ged eawr meal i' peace. No costly danties grace or booard, But plain an' hooamly fare; But sich as 'tis, we're never short, There's allus some to spare. Aw'm poor as far as riches gooa, Av'm but o' low degree; But if contentment ceawnts as wealth, Ther's nobry mooar nor me. Booath me an' t' wife known t' sweets o' life, For eawr three childer yon Mek ts' world a Heaven to hur an' me; God bless 'ern every one! BILL 0' JACK'S

div.head: CREWE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE CREWE TRAGEDY.

THE MURDERED MAN'S PROPERTY. An incident in connection with the Crewe murder took place at Crewe on Tuesday night, when Mr. Gibson offered for sale the murdered man's property. Davies' widow drove in from The Hough in a little pony trap in which her husband was murdered, but she did not pre- sent herself in the sale-room. The autioneer avoided reference to the crime remarking that there was no necessity to allude to the circumstances under which the property came into the market. A shop and bakehouse in Market-st. reached £1,450, but were withdrawn. Two shops in Victoria-st., in one of which Davies carried on his business, were also withdrawn at £9lO. According to the deceased's vritt the property was divisible among his children equally, the two lads who murdered their father being mentioned in the will.

He had sent in hi& papers and resigned his com- mission. Private affairs, he said, required his pre- sence in England, and he had had done his work. All through the mutiny he had carried his corps to victory, and for months afterwards he had performed services which entitled him to some distinction.

But his rewards never came as he, perhaps, expected. He had received medals and praises but other military distinction was not for him. SO he determined to resign his troop and had obtained leave for a month to go up to Simla. Here he met General Deane. The General was satisfied that he had at last met the man whose unerring aim, whose coolness in the midst of a storm of bullets in the street of Delhi had certainly saved Sir William's life. But, besides this, the General was haunted by a suspicion that he had seen the man under different circumstances. "Where could this man and I have met before This was the question the senior officer put to him- self many times. His inquiries did not lead to much, however. There was a confused idea that the officer and a certain Sowar were one and the same man, but no clue guided itself to the General's mind. One day the conversation turned upon military executions, and General Deane, being asked, related the curious experience which ho had had. He narrated the incidents already set forth respecting the escape of Sergeant Layton, and the extraordinaly substitution of the offending officer. "I tried all in my power to get the man off," con- tinued the General. "I made it even a personal matter, and put the circumstances as favourably as I could. There was some error somewhere. lam glad the poor fellow escaped; he only acted upon impulse, though a very reprehensible one. I have often wondered what became of him."
"Enlisted, probably, and got shot in the mutiny," suggested one present:
1"—No. I faiicy I heard of him," said an old colonel. "I took a great interest in his case, for I knew him well, and he had a deuced pretty wife." "By-the-by, what became Of her ?" asked tho General.

" Sho went to England, I heard. But misfortunes never come alone. The ship was wrecked, and many perished. There was a good deal of talk about her at one time. She was was more sinned against than sinnino• I believe."

"1 quite agree with you," said Captain Rush- leigh. ";But what became of her? Waa she lost? Do you happen to remember the ship's name ? " "Well, hardly," replied the person addressed. "I became acquainted with the circumstances throuah the surgeon. I have no doubt her husband will turn up some day. He is one of those fellows who have as many lives as a cat." "I should like to see him," remarked the captain, as he rose and left the room. "I am truly sorry his wife is dead. I knew her well; and liked her very much. Excuse me, gentlemen." He quitted the room, and the conversation took another turn, but the General murmured— "I am sure I have mot that ran before. I must endeavour to find out where"

CHAPTER XX. TEMPTATION.-A EI:DE SMOCK. To say that George Collier was not startled when he perceived Sandy Sam so close to him, and at such a time, would be wronging tho signalman. He did feel very considerably alarmed, but in an instant he had made up his mind to ignore all unpleasantness, and thus endeavour to throw the leader of the " strike " off his guard. "Hallo, mate, what brings you here?" he said, assuming a cheerful tone, though he was far from feeling cheerful just then. "Come out and tell ur the news."

The other never answered, and Collier, with a fast-beating heart, went on with his duties, and apparently ignored Sandy Sam, who was still in ambush. The strong man—armed as he was—was rather subdued by the manner of his reception. Ilad he had the least excuse he would have knocked the signalman on the head; but he could not venture to strike him defenceless. There was a certain feeling of fair play particularly when he was discovered.

It may be almost unaccountable, but this man, who would have five minutes previously wounded or even killed his enemy, now hesitated to stir a finger against him. But he did not abate one jot of his real purpose, nevertheless. He had succeeded in partly stopping the works. The men had listened to him, and had voted him a liberal subscription from their wages and the union funds. This salary, gained for doing nothing, for merely preaching a crusade against capital—which is so easy to do, as long as funds are forthcoming—suited Mr. Sandy Sam perfectly. Ile had done something, but not enough. The signalmen and engine-drivers had to be brought out. Higher wages were wanted. The men must have beer and the wives must have dresses—particularly the former; and the signalman also must join the movement—" One for all, and all for one." "Come out, Sandy,' said George Collier; "come out, man. Don't sneak up there as if you were doing something you were ashamed of. What do you want with me ?" "None of your gammon," replied the sulky striker. "Look here. The men up at the works is all corain' out to-morrow. Not a man will work for that yonder." " Meanin' Sir Walter, I suppose," said Collier. "Yes; meanin' him. Now," continued the man, "I'm the mouthpiece of the union—" "And a very dirty mouthpiece you are," muttered Collier.
"And I'm going to speak to you. for your good. We have promises front lots of your mates. We want you to join us. If you do, all well, and your wages will be raised: If not—"
'Who will rise them F " asked Collier, leaning on the lever. "Why him; the chairman—Watson. We'll make him, or we'll know why." . . . _ _

" two can play at that game," replied Collier. "He may get men to work the line and the shops. Where will you be then?" " We'll be all right. 'We're not goin' to stand his interference. He is makin' his fortune out of us. We are killin' ourselves and starving by inches for him, while he wallows in gold and finery. Now we are not slaves—are we ? " . "Not yet." acquiesced Collier._ _ _

Well, then, We've come out like men and Eng- lishmen ready to fight the battle for wages. Are you goin' to join us, or are you not ? " "Suppose I said not ? ' asked the signalman, quietly. "Well then we'd mark you, picket you, and cut your wires and bring you on your knees." "But you'll ruin the railway and kill a train full of passengers, perhaps," remonstrated Collier, who was talking against time, for he was thinking how best he might dissuade this man, or outwit him. "That's what we would like to do—at least, to ruin Watson. The passengers must look out. Next week the drivers and firemen will come out, and then we'll try for the guards. You must come, or, by Jingo, we'll not leave a box on the line."
"Ye can't hurt the boxes, anyway," said the signalman, tentatively, and wishing someone would come up and assist him. "They have done ye na harm."

"Oh, can't we hurt them?" sneered the brute. "Have ye never heard of blasting-powder or gun. cotton? Can't ye hurt the boxes? Who blew 14 Tom Jenard the other day at the forge?" "Do you mean to tell use that you would do thatsli Why, we're all in your power and might be destroyed any minute." "Dead men tdil no tales," rejoined the arch-striker,. significantly. "Our plans are made, our mines an laid, and in one minute I could lift you over the trcoi yonder." "Well, then, I must give in, I suppose. But what do you want me to do?" "That's right, I thought you would assist us. I will swear you in. Come, you must take the oath not to betray us, and tell tales." "I'm not going to tell any tales. You can do what you like with me, only no uadermining." "That's just it. Look here. Mind you've swore on it.. The chairman is goin' to-morrow to inspect the oft of line near Broadbent. He has this after- noon refused all our demands, and taken on new hands. The men at Broadbent have been dismissed. We are gum' to pay him and his people out." " How ? " inquired emeer. "Never you mind. I've got all the plans in my pocket, and they're not likely to be seen till the time comes. You will know the time the special is due, and you must signal it at once to Broadbent, so that all may be ready." "But I can't till I know what for," said Collier, who was racking his brain to find an excuse to upset Sandy Sam, but any struggle would only result in his own discomfiture. The relief man was not due for hours, and hero was a diabolical crime, the outcome of a long series of fancied, or partly real, oppression. What;the men wero about to do Collier could only guess. Most likely wreck the train, and he, the trusted signalman, was to be the scapegoat. No, better the first than thus basely desert his post. George Collier made up his mind to play "foxy," as he would have expressed it. _ All was fair under such circumstances.

div.p: NO ROBBERY.
BY HENRY FRITI3. Author of " 71e Mystery of ,3loor Farm," 1173-4 Tr 'lugs opthe Wind," "Through Flood, Through Fiie,4c., &c.
CIIAPTER XIX• TAKING OF DELISI-A 000 D SEIM

Wu have been a long time ab'sent from India, where stirring events had been daily taking place. While our attention has been concentrated upon Mrs. Layton and the schemes she was weaving, Sir William Deane has been through many adventures and seen some service. .

It does not come within the seope of this narrative to detail all the events which happened in that eventful period at Delhi, nor to do more than to touch upon the circumstances connected with the siege. We must, however, devote some littleapace to this period of history in order that the subsequent narrative may be understood. September, 1557, was an eventful month in our Indian territory, and Colonel Deane had been distin- guishing himself, as every one expected he would. He had never again encountered the Sower he had met the evening of his arrival in camp, and the impres,;ion upon his mind was that the man had deserted. The breaching batteries were completed early in the month, and for two nights and days they poured in a destructive tire upon the city. The prepara- tions for the assault were vigorously pushed on, and trenches were opened, and the Engineers worked un- molested until it was too late for the enemy to pre- vent them.

On the 13th the breaches were reported practi- cable, and as colonel Deane was sleeping calmly amid all the din of bombardment, a light touch upon his arm awoke him instantly. The colonel immediately leaped to his feet as if ashamed of being "caught napping," and perceived an orderly holding a lanthorn, and around him were standing several officers, all busily engaged in read- ing the orders which had arrived. " What is it? When is the assault to take place?" inquired the colonel. "As early as ever we can. Six o'clock is the hour named, but no one can tell for certain," replied one of the officers. "But the Rifles are to make the inspection to-night, and we shall have plenty of occmation to-morrow." It was even as he said. No sooner had the dark- ness begun to gather round than the Engineers, escorted and covered by a detachment of the 60th Rifles; came from under cover. Ten o'clock struck, and the'men moved out quietly and without !noise to the glaeis. A ladder was at hand, and two officers descended into the ditch, and. then proceeded to mount to the summit of the breach.

It was a bold and hazardous duty, but there was no flinching. The young Engineer officer mounted and had nearly gained the top when a loose stone or some other loose object clattering roused the enemy, and they came running along to the breach. Lying close, the Engineers noted the state of the bastions and the condition of the breach. But the enemy uufortunately showed no signs of returning. There was nothing for it, therefore, but to retire the way they had come, and the Engineers accordingly got up and descended the breach. Under a galling fire they hurried back with the Information that the breach was practicable, and their report was immediately conveyed to head- quarters. The necessary orders were at once despateliod and arrived as had been related, after some had sought what rest they could find for the last night some of them were to pass on earth. There were four columns of attack, and, the Cashmere Gate was particularly entrusted to the Engineers, while Kissingunge, a village on the road to Delhi, was occupied by the goorkahs. About daylight the action began, and the Goorkahs had the first of it, and then the fight became general. The Cashmere bastion was carried by escalade, and not a man used his rifle until ho had gained a footing on the walls, when Colonel Deane found himself' confronted by a strong force of rebels.

They did not remain long though, and soon the Cashmere Gate was blown open, and the artillery was ordered up. The oxen will not move, the drivers are unwilling, so the officers have to prod man and beast with their swords until they consent to proceed, and Delhi was entered. It was here that an incident occurred which had a very considerable influence upon the officer with whose fortunes we are just now concerned; and this brought him into contact with the mysterious individual whom he had already noticed outside the city. It was no !joke to cross the open space by the church, for round shot and bullets were flying as thickly as can be imagined, and the rebels took good care to' keep concealed. There was a picket of the 52nd Foot close by, and the men were get- ting hit just because they were too tired and careless to take any trouble to get under cover. Colonel Deane rode up and remonstrated with the men who werevery lax in discipline when not actually engaged, and were so tired and unruly, that they seized upon any brandy or other liquor and drank greedily, notwithstanding all remonstrances. Not very far from where the colonel was standing was a tree, and in the branches of it was perched a Sepoy, who:managed to avoid every shot the men fired at him. He was busily engaged shooting at the British, and certainly two soldiers had fallen to his am, when the colonel appeared.

dose by .were some natives squatting under shelter, and one of these had a long gun. The man in the tree was about to take aim, and just as he did so, the colonel became aware of the danger ho was in. But he was unable to conceal himself, and did not hurry away. Another moment would have sealed his fate, when an officer of Irregulars sprang to his feet, and regardless of the bullets which were flying about, snatched a musket, levelled, and fired at the Sepoy.. The man in the tree fell upon the roof of a house close by, and rolled from it to the ground, a corpse. He had been shot through the forehead. The colonel was saved. Without hesitation he turned to thank the native officer, when to his astonishment the man hurried away without even a salute, or acknowledgment of any kind. "To what corps does that officer belong 2" inquired the colonel. "The Guides, I believe, sir," was the reply. "Fetch him to my quarters presently. I'm sure I have seen him before. He saved my life at any rate." But the man never appeared. Still his featiares remained impressed upon the colonel's memory, and when years afterwards they met again, he recognised him.

It was after the mutiny had been suppressed, and Sir William Deane was homeward bound. The great struggle was over, and when all was quiet, Sir William, then a General, was up at Simla. He was about to leave India, after several years active and garrisoriservice, and just before he quitted the station he was introduced to Captain Rushleigh of the Irregular Cavalry. Captain Rushleigh was a fine, well-formed man, his bronzed cheeks and a deep, but not disfiguring, scar upon his brow bearing rtestimony to the service ho had seen. When General Deane was introduced, the officer greeted him formally, but the General b 24 "I am pleased to make your acquaintance, CaPain Rushleigh, for I have Lheard of your many acts of daring and skilful disposition of your men." Rushleigh bowed 'and murmured a few words expressive of the pleasure he experienced from the General's praise. " I think we have met before," continued Sir William "Surely, you were at Delhi !'• The captain of Irregulars would have evaded this direct inquiry had it been possible, but he was in the midst of a group of men who had seen and recog- nised his exploits, and to deny his identity was now impossible. He therefore assented, and was about to change the conversation, when Sir William continued— _ _

"Stop, sir. ltrust you will not consider me in- trusive, but:your features are quite tominr to me. Is it possible that I have the pleasure of seeing the officer who I caraot but consider saved my life at Delhi?"
"I think I did pot a Pandy in a tree who was Llkinr, aim at you, General.: }tut I deserve nt credit—"

"I beg your pardon. You will permit tne to con- sider my life worth something to myself and family at any rate. I have often wished to meet that officer. Captain Rushleigh, I thank you warmly as a soldier, and—if you will permit me—as a friend." The captain had no alternative. He was a reserved and undemonstrative man. He seldom associated intimately with any up at Simla, but with the officers of his own regiment he was very popular and much liked by the men. Under the circumstances he could do no less than assent, comforting himself with the assurance that he was about to quit India, for a time at any rate.

"I don't think I can assist ye much,' he said. " I shall not be on duty at that time to-morrow, and my mate won't tell " Your mate must tell. I'll take good care of him, for he is already in it, my man; and, had I thought you were so squeamish, rd have blown up your Jack-in, the-Box before this !" This was said so fiercely that Collier at once per- ceived the man was not to be trifled with. If assist- ance would only come! But Collier had only himself to depend upon, and now it had become a trial of wit against brute force, of brain against hands. A sudden idea struck the signalman. But what if the plan, so suddenly con- ceived, should fail? Still he thought he might save himself. "It's not necessary for me to appear in the• matter at all, Sam," he said, affecting a friendlY tone. "Why, you are a clever chap, and up to all kinds of games. You've no fear, like me." "You're about right there," said Sandy Sam, complacently. "I'm just as tough as iron, and care for nobody nor nothin'." "Just so. Now don't you think it would be much. more useful for you to learn the beats and signals a little? Then you could come here and do what you liked, and I needn't appear in the matter." "Are ye afraid, ye white-livered muff?" "Well, I'm not afraid exactly; but ye see I've no grievance at aIL And there is no excuse for mete appear discontented. Now you have a reason, and if I teach you the signals and beats you can work the whole thing like a general, as you are, al td throw them off the scent." "I see," muttered Sandy Sam. "Go on." "I mean this," continued Collier. "Here are the instruments; you can always use them, and not only now, but in future, it may be very useful for ye to know them. If you tie me up to-morrow I. shall be out of it. I won't peach, you may depend, for my own sake, and you can arrange everything." "And be independent of you, besides," said Sandy Sam. "Who can tell whether you would telegraph correctly or not?" The proposal had evidently met with his approval', but he would not give way all at once. "Exactly so," replied Collier, answering his last remark. "I think ye may depend on me; but ye want a thing done ye had better do it your- self. It costs no more, and will answer better, and save my credit to help you in future. D'ye sees tote ?" a Right you are," responded the " striker,° with a wink. "I'll put some of them into *- hole. When can ye begin to tell me the telegraph —now ? " Collier affected to consider, and, after a pause, he replied, glancing at the clock— " Let me see. My mate will be here in an hour or so. I think we shall have time; but first I must signal the goods train." "None of your larks," said Sam. itisTo peaching to the next box, or by the living Jingo as sure as I see anyone coming here I'll blow your brains out. I have had my eye on you." George Collier felt his plan had failed so far. Ile had thought to give the next box a hint when the relief man was due, and thus secure help. But if the " man were an accomplice the result would be dis- astrous to himself after all. In any case there was no help that way now. "You may kill me if you please. I'm not going to wire anything but the train. Look here. We have so many beats for the passenger train, so many for an engine by itself, and so many for a goods train. The special is five beats. Like this.' Collier detached the wires from the instruments and as he was touching them he received a smart shock that made him jump. :He uttered an exclamation of joy as he pretended to fix them again. "Why, here's a better plan than all," he re- marked with scarce-concealed satisfaction. "Look here. But wait a minute. Let me see if the battery is full charged." He ascertained beyond a doubt that " a very- powerful current was traversing the wires. Then, turning to the ringleader of the conspiracy, be

said— " You can hear the beats and almost what they are saying in the next box. Listen." "Gammon," exclaimed the man. "how can ye hear voices a mile away ? " "By wire. Can't ye hear through the trunk of a tree or along an iron rail ? " "That's true," remarked Sandy Sam, who was ne scientist, but who was well acquainted with the acoustW properties of timber and iron, though the telephone was not invented. "That's true, and it will save trouble and time if I listen." "Just come and try; here, catch hold," said Collier, trembling with eagerness. "No larks," said Sandy Sam, threateningly. "You'll not touch me, mind." "I won't go near you; I'll stand here. Now, when I tell you put a wire in each ear, not too tight, and hold them there. I'll see that nothing interrupts the sound. Come." The man unsuspectingly took one wire from the instrument, and at the given signal suddenly clutched both, and with an expression of anger, put them to his ears. The current, permitted by Collier to flow with full force, darted through him like a flash of lightning, and he fell back senseless on the floor of the box. "Now for the papers," said Collier, "and when-ray mate turns up I'll tackle him too, and inform Sir Walter. That's a good lob done." The papers were soon in George's hands; the man never moved. The electric current had done its work well. Sandy Sam lay apparently lifeless beneath the levers and the signal instruments. (To be continued.)

That was all

right, and he had nothing more to say about it, as Sergeant Shaw had taken upon himself the responsibil- ity of giving in his resignation. He had only to deal with Jones. He was afraid that when Jones was appointed, some members of the Watch Committee were not alive to the antecedents of the gentleman they were about to elevate to the position of sergeant. If they had referred to the report book— Aldeyman IlinnisoN, interrupting, said Councillcr Pierpoint was wandering out of his latitude. He was not discussing a question of paymen t,and he should be stopped. Councillor H. Roeirnan : Councillor Pierpoint is giving reasons for the course he is taking. He is, I submit, about to adduce reasons why 31s. if too much to pay to Sergeant Jones. Alderman HannisoN: Thetis questioning the action of the Watch Committee. Councillor PIERPOINT said he did not want to do any- thing that was irregular, or which should weaken the position of the Chief Constable, but he had a perfect right to call attention to the fact that the Committee had promoted a man over the heads of other people, a man witlra very indifferent repopt against his name. He was going to read these reports. Alderman Hammon objected to the reports being read. Councillor PIERPOINT : Alderman Harrison is not con- ducting the meeting, and I ask you (the Mayor) to keep him as quite as possible. (Laughter.) In March. 1886 (28th March), Inspector Berry reported Sergeant Jones for being strongly under the influence of drink. ' Alderman HARRISON: It is cruel to rake up these ante- cedents. It is very unjust. Councillor PIERPOINT : That islyhat I want to avoid, and if you will assure me that I am acting unjustly I will sit down at once and leave these unfortunate reports. The MAYOR: I should like to say that the man fell grieviously through drink, but he wa,s reduced in rank and suffered. He has since turned out to be a most excellent officer. This has all been dragged up before his face at the Watch Committee, and he has promised that such a thing shall not happen again. Councillor PIERPOINT : I want to know whether the Committee, before they appointed P.C. Jones to the office of sergeant, had made sufficient enquiries with reference to the men in the force, men who had been in it a number of years, against whom no report had been made, and who had always been looked upon as zealous officers. I want to know if you have appointed the best man in P.C. Jones. That is all I wanted to get at. Alderman Hammon said they were extremely careful • before they appointed Jones. They made every possible enquiry; but as they must be aware they must depend mainly upon what Mr. Hunt said, as he had had more experience of the men than they had. He assured Councillor Pierpoint that they took all precautions, and they questioned and cross-questioned Mr. Hunt as to the policy and propriety of appointing Jones to the position. He satisfied them and more than satisfied them that it °was the most desirable thing they could do. He pro- nounced Jones to be an excellent officer, and said he had the fullest confidence in him, and, therefore, they sanctioned the appointment as intimated in the minutes. Councillor Dr. CANNELL seconded the amendment, and said he would like to ask one or two questions. He should say nothing about Seigeant .Shaw, but was it true that Mr. Hunt refused to give a character to ex- Constable Jones when' he applied to the Wigan Town Council, to Messrs. Walker and Sons, and to Mr. Alder- man Harrison for a situation? Councillor H. ROBERTS supported the amendment, be- cause undoubtedly the appointment of Jones was the most unsavoury one in the force, and in the town, that had been made for years. He said that without the slightest hesitation. The appointment was most unpopu- lar in the force—(hear, hear)—it was also most unpopu- lar in the town. The question had been thoroughly ventilated in the town without anything being closured and what Councillor Pierpoint was about to read was as commonly known as a daily newspaper. It was in the mouth of everyone in the town who took an interest in municipal matters that the Watch Committee had promoted a man who was dismissed from the force three and a half years ago for the offence which had been mentioned that night. What the Watch Committee had done was a reflection upon the force as much as to say that there was not a man in the force— 'Councillor liovroN: Was Jones dismissed or did he resign? Alderman HARRISON: He was dismissed. There is no (doubt about that: Councillor H. ROBERTS: It is a reflection upon the force that there is no one in it who by length of service and good conduct is not better entitled to the position than the me.n named. Councillor Smile GREEN suggested to the Committee that they should re-consider the matter. It would be Infinitely better than taking a vote upon a painful matter of that 'description. Alderman StrrroN agreed with the proposal of Coun- cillor Green, but at the same time, as a member of the Watch Committee, he would be very reluctant to come there and move any amendment to their resolutions. He was satisfied that the Committee had fully, fairly, and properly considered the question before arriving at a conclusion. Aleerman HARRISON: This resolution, as you know, is altogether illegal, and has no right to be submitted. Councillor MONKS: The Town Clerk says it can. The Town Crmax : Yes, with regard to the amount of wages. The amendment was then submitted to the Council, the voting being as follows : For. . Against. Alderman Holmes The Mayor „ Burgess Alderman Sutton Councillor Monks 911 Harrison Pierpoint Councillor Bolton Cannell „ Tinsley t „ Beaman „ Heaton „ Flood „ Ashton ~ Garner „ Muir „ Roberts .„ Percival The MAYOR : The figures are nine for, nine against. I shall support the minutes. lie therefore gave his casting vote against the amend- ment which was lost. Councillor Roamers said that after the expression of opinion that evening, it was extremely desirable that the matter should be re-considered, and he would, therefore, move a further amendment. He begged to move that the minates be confirmed with the exception of the one relating to the appointment of Francis Jones as sergeant at 318. per week. Alderman SUTTON That cannot be done. Councillor ROBERTS: Very well. I move an amend- , ment.to the effect that he be appointed sergeant at 255. Alderman Sorrow: That cannot be done. It is against the rules. The MAYOR: The scale fixed by the Council is 31s. Councillor ROBERTS: I want to move an amendment that is in order, and I am perfectly prepared to abide by your instruction in regard to the tenor of it. The MAYOR: If you will move that he have 325. a week you can do it. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS said he would move that the orders for the payment of accounts be not confirmed. The only reason he had for moving that amendment was that after the expressions of opinion which had been given utter- ance to that the matter demanded re-consideration, it only mat dtere:heonutitod bet h e mC ou ruen cai ml apnl yd dt sec u ratess e dp a av nerds Lc ho na t_ sidered by the Committee than it appeared to have been. (Hear, hear.) If the police force had not within its ranks a man who by length of service and good con- duct had rendered himself more qualified for the post than the man whose name was before the Council, then,, he said, and he said it advisedly, the condition of the 'police force was not creditable to anybody connected with it. (Hear, hear.) But he refused for one moment to believe that it was in that condition. He believed there had been a little bit of personal feeling with regard to the appointment of Jones. There was such a thing as favouritism, and that was one of the very things which tended more than anything else to ruin the discipline and proper spirit which should exint in the police force If that sort of thing had existed in connection with the appointment of Jones, the Council ought to take to itself at once his amendment, and say "We will not submit to this kind of thing." If the Watch Committee had any sense of self-respect they would refuse to be guided by the dictum of one of their own officers. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JENKINS seconded the amendment, saying that he did so because it was quite clear from the obser- vations which had been made by various members of the Council that the proceedings of the Watch Committee, so far as could be gathered from the resolution, were not by any means satisfactory. (Hear, hear.) He should suggest that before the Committee adopted the recom- mendations of the Chief Constable they should make enquiries in other boroughs as to the mode in which matters were conducted, and see whether the Chief Con- stables in other boroughs had vested in them such arbi- trary powers. The Mayon read the following amendment, which he stated had been moved by Councillor Roberts :—" That the minutes of the Watch Committee referring to the payment of accounts, be net confirmed." It was pointed out that this amendment did not affect the appointment of Jones. Councillor ROBERTS said he proposed that amendment with the view of having that matter with regard to Sergeant Jones referred back. If that amendment did not meet it, there was no need to press it any further. The MAYOR : No it does not.

- Councillor ROBERTS: Very well; I wish to move one that does. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk says the matter having„ been discussed and settled by the Council, is not now open for further discussion. Councillor ROBERTS: Then we are in this position, that this appointment is confirmed by your casting vote. The TOWN CLERK: Yes. Councillor ROBERTS asked the Mayor to give an under- taking that the matter should be re-considered in Com- mittee. All he could ask was the Mayor's personal assurance that the Committee would go into the matter again. The MAYOR said he would certainly give that assurance, but there were several words that he could not quite agree with which had been used during the discussion.
