It had been said that it was an insulf to theforce that no other man could be found to take the position. Councillor llonsars said he did not ask the Mayor to endorse all he had said. The MAYOR said there were two or three splendid men whom be would like to see promoted, but When he had mentioned them he had always been met with the answer that their education had been neglected. Councillor Romurrs said he would leave the matter Ithere, accepting the Mayor's personal assurance that it would be re-considered. Alderman SUTTON said he did not see how the matter could be re-considered. That resolution bad been come to by the Committee, and the Council had no right to question it, or to propose any amendment. Seeing that the resolution bad been eonfirmed, there was nothing for it now but to watch how Jones conducted himself as a sergeant, and if he did not do so in a proper manner, it would be for the Watch Committee to give him notice to leave the position he occupied. Although there might be a personal feeling existing ' amongst the police, it cer- tainly would create even a still worse feeling if the Coun- cil were to put Jones aside and appoint someone else in his place. Councillor BOLTON said he thought it might be left in the hands of the Committee. . .

..... Councillor FLOOD said he claimed the right of being heard on that question. He did not believe in the doc- trine of ramming a thing down one's throat and accept- ing it as true. He begged to move an amendment that the whole of the minutes be referred back to the tom- mittea for further consideration. AldermanliertarsoN : You cannot do it.

. - -- --- Councillor FLOOD : There is just as much power, I presume, to move that the whole of the minutes be sub- mitted back for consideration as to move that only one resolution be referred back? .

Councillor CANNEtt : Can the Watch Committee spend the ratepayers' money without the authority of the Town Council ? The MAYOR : No. Councillor FLOOD: Can these minutes be referred back for consideration?

The TOWN CLERK: No, sir. Councillor FLOOD: That will do. Councillor FLEMING : If it could be done, I should like to support that. The MAYOR: I promise Councillor Roberts I will bring this matter up at the next meeting of the Watch Com- mittee. _ . .
Councillor Morras : Upon my word, Ido not see the use it is bringing up these minutes. Alderman BURGESS : Nor I either; let us have no more Watch Committee minutes. _

The minutes were then adopted. NEW Boum, Sm. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee pro- posed that the plans of the following buildings, Sm., be approved :—Six houses in Forshaw-st., for Mr. John Appleton ;eight houses in Cartwright-st., for Mr. George Wallington; cellar under shop and premises at the ' corner of Aiken-st. and Priestley-st., for Messrs. Peter Walker and Son; office behind the" Blue Bell" Inn, in Market Place for Messrs. Greene.% Whitley, and Com- pany, Limited; four houses and one shop in Birchall-st., for Mr. James Hill; alteration to house in Museum-st., for Mr. Reginald Silcock ; shop in Sankey-st., for Messrs. Samuel Claff and Goodman, (conditionally). Also that Mr. Councillor Henry Roberts be appointed a member of this committee. Alderman Surrox moved. and Councillor Mons seconded the confirmation of the minutes. • Councillor Moxxs, referring to the proposed improve- ment of shop property at the bottom of Legh-street, said it was desirable that negotiations should take place with a view to having the premises set back to the line of the otheepart of Sankey-st. Alderman Surrox replied that the Committee had approached the owner of the property on the subject, and he resolutely declined to comply with their request. The minutes were confirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The report of the Inspector to the above-named Com- mittee stated that 53 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 52 cases for 127 children; and 19 cases had been taken be- fore the magistrates, and fines inflicted in each case. 34 case's were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the public elemebtary schools during the month of June was 7,612, corresponding period last year. 7,3o7—increase 305. The minutes were approved on the motion of Coun- cillor FLEituto, seconded by Councillor &raw Gnaw.

PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommended that Golden-square be paved with setts ; that the tender of the Warrington Slate Company, Limited, to supply 10,000 blue bricks, at 48s. 3d. per 1.000 be accepted ; and that in the opinion of the Committee, it is desirable that the provisions of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, relating to matters within the province of this Committee be adopted. Councillor FLEMING moved that the minutes be ap- proved. \ Councillor HEATON seconded, and the proposi- tion was agreed to.

TRH SANITARY COMMITTER. The minutes of this Committee contained the following items :—Report of the Borough Treasurer that he had received from the County Treasurer the proportionate amounts under the Contagious Diseases ( Animals) Act of £73 7s. 2d. and under the Food and Drugs Act of £l5 7s. 3d. ; that the tender of Mr. John Cooper to supply provender for horses, during the next three months, be accepted ; that the premises of Mr. John Ford, as des- cribed in the Declaration of the Inspector, be declared infected with pleuro-pneumonia, and that the animals on such premises' be slaughtered; that the Town Clerk be instructed to take the necessary steps for the adoption by

. , thd Council of all the sectidns of the Infectitms Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890 ; that in the opinion of this Com- mittee, it is desirable that the sanitary provisions of the Public Health Acts, Amendment Act, 1890, be adopted by. the Council; that the tender of Monks Hall Sz Com- pany, Limited, to supply one ton of hoop iron at £8 be accepted. Alderman Moaciess, in moving the adoption of the minute, said he coo fowl to *ate that there had been an outbreak of pluro-pneumonia in the borough, but it would be some satisfaction to the Council to know that the cost to the town would be very small. He had every reason to believe that the charges for slaughtering a large herd of cattle would fall on the County of Chester. The proposition was seconded by Alderman SUTTON. Councillor JENKirrs referred to a practice of throwing slops from houses in Manchester-road into the thorough- fare. Alderman Btrimass, replying to the discussion, said that in reference to the observations of Mr. Jenkins as to the tlirowing out of slops in front of houses, in Man- chester-rd., he was sorry to say that in all probability the people had no other means of disposing of them. He agreed in condemning the practice, but it arose through the fact that we had yet in Warrington a number of back to back houses. The minutes were then confirmed. TDB LIBRARY AND MUSEUM. The minutes of the Museum, Library and Arts Com- mittee showed as follows :—Visitors to the Museum, for the month of July, 2,854, increase 4 per cent., compared with July, 1889; books issued in read- ing-room, 1,107, increase 15 per cent.; books issued in lending department 1,953, increase 5 per cent. Report of the following gifts for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—Notes and Queries, two vols., in continuation from Mr. R. Pierpoint -, Photographs of Ship Canal workings, from the Town Clerk; Clive's Shorthand, 1821, and two other works, from Mr. W. H. Woodcock.—The Chairman announced that he wished to present to the art gallery, the marble figure of 'Rachel," by J. Warrington Wood, which had been purchased by Mr. Chorley, at a sale in London. It was resolved that the Committee accept with great pleasure the handsome'donation offered by Mr. Robert Davies, and desire to convey to him their unanimous and hearty thanks for the same; and also that the best thanks of the committee be tendered to Mr. Charles Chorley, for the great Interest he has shown, and the trouble he has had in connection with the acquisition of the above work of art. Councillor Morms, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he thought the thanks of the Council were due to Mr. Robert Davies for the very handsome gift he had made the Corporation. The Borough Treasurer also was deserving of thanks for so generously assisting in the purchase of the work. Councillor ROBERTS seconded the proposition and the minutes were confirmed.

CEMETERY column-mu. The Registrar, at a meeting of this Cornnaittee.reported that the interments for the past four weeks were : Adults, 28; minors, 47; stillborn and premature, 10. And for the corresponding period last year :—Adults, 30; minors, 56; stillbarn and premature, 11. The receipts for the past four weeks were reported to be £6O 14s. 5d., and for the corresponding period last year, £64 is. 7d.. On the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor JENKINS, the minutes were agreed to.
TOWN HALL, YARN, AND BATHS COMMrITEE.- TIIE QIJES- -- - -

TION OF THE BATHS. The Bathkeeper, at a meeting held on the 21st August, reported that the Income from the baths during the past four weeks was £32 2s. Bd., and for the corresponding period last year £22 7s. At a meeting held on the 7th August, it was resolved that Mr. Alderman Wright be appointed a member of this Committee.—At another meeting it was resolved that tho tender of Messrs. Patte- son, of Manchester, to prepare and lay Roman marble mosaic pavement in the vestibule of the Town Hall be accepted, subject to certain alterations in the designs; that the Young Men's Christian Association be allowed the free use of the first-class swimming bath for one evening for the purpose of a gala; that twelve dozen towels be provided for the use of bathers in the second- class plunge bath, on a charge of id. per towel; and that six large roller towels be provided for the free use of bathers; that a suitable washing tab be provided in each plunge bath for the free use of bathers; that soap bti pro- vided for use in the private slipper baths; and that an additional £5 be voted to the bands for playing in the park on Sundays during the remainder of the season. The MAYOR, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes, remarked that with ieference to the proposal to lay mosaic pavement in the vestibule, the Committee took a considerable amount of time in selecting the best people to carry out the work. . Councillor BOLTON seconded the proposition. Councillor ROBERTS said he was very glad to see that the Committee were acting in a better spirit towards the baths ; but the second class plunge bath was still a long way from what it ought to be. Twopence was charged for admission. If the Committee made the place free they would not be conferring a very great boon,but they might at least provide towels. The MAYOR said the Committee were supplying six very large roller towels. It was• only when a person wanted a special one that a charge was made. Councillor Roamers said that considering the contemp- tible accessories which existed at the twopenny bath, the Committee might offer a free towel as an inducement to to people come. He moved that the words "on a charge ofd. per towel "be left out of the resolution. The MAYOR said that the Committee really intended to do what Councillor Roberts suggested, by providing the large towels. The charge would be made only when a bather wanted a towel to himself.

, Councillor RODBRTS : But whynot go the whole hog? It is not worth. while charging a halfpenny. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JRNangs seconded the amendment, and drew attention to the want of ventilation in the first class bath. • Councillor IrtnrEcn thought it would be a gracious, ant on the part of the Council not to charge for the towels. Twopence was a great sum for many working lads. He supported the amendment and hoped that every person who used the bathe would be supplied with a clean towel. Councillor Mum said that the baths had been very • much improved since the present Committee had been in office. (Hear, hear.) Alderman StrrroN said that, seeing that it was very probable the baths would have to be re-built or• re-con- constructed, it would be as well to let matters remain in the position the Committee wished. Councillor Mornts, referring to the question of "music in the park," said it was sufficiently evident that it met: a public want. Therefore, he thought the matter ought net to be left, as it had been for the last few years,. to three gentlemen to manage. He was of opinion that it came within the scope and duties of the Committee, and he should be glad if they could see their way to take it up, and in November make such arraug•ements•as. would ensure the musical performances being continued from year to year. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Hantnsorr said he hoped Councillor Roberts would not persist in his amendment. Councillor Homers said he considered there was a very important principle at stake in the matter, but seeing that all the respectable and intelligent members of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee left it some time ago, he did not wish to be toe bard upon it in, its denuded condition. (Laughter.) Councillor BOLTON said that the Committee would like. to issue the towels free of charge if the Council would support them in their action. What they had done now was to offer, what had never been offered before, a towel for a id., and if that concession were appreciated, the next step would be to do away with the charge alto- gether. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR remarked that for many years the second class baths had had no towels. Now the Committee wish to provide six large towels as an experiment. They were quite prepared to accept suggestions. If 2d. was considered; too great a charge for admission, he would like to see it reduced to id., or even made free. On the matter being put to the vote the following voted for the amendment :—Abderman Burgess, Coun- cillors Pierpoint, Fleming, Green Beaman, Jenkins, Roberts, Flood, Garner, Muir, and Faircloth. The following voted against the amendment :,--The Mayor, Aldermen Holmes and Sutton, and Councillors Monks, Bolton, Cannell, Percival, Ashton Heaton. The minutes as amended, were then adopted.

OAS COMMITTIM At a meeting of the Gas Committee it was reported that the average illuminating power of the gas during the past four weeks was equal to 18°34 candles at both works. It was resolved that the following tenders for the supply of coal for the next twelve months be ac- cepted :—The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, 3,000 tons : The Moss Hall Co., 4,000; Cross, Tetley and Co., 4,000 tons. The minutes were passed:on the motion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this Committee it was resolved, "That , the common seal of the borough be affixed to the agree- ment made between the Corporation and the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Limited, the Whitecross Co., Limited, and Rylands Bros., Limited, relating to the water supply of those companies." "That in com- pliance with the requirements of the Local Government Board, the application for the sanction of that Board to the grant of the plot of land to the trustees of the War- rington Infirmary be made by memorial, and that the common seal of the borough be affixed thereto." On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman Surrox, the minutes were confirmed, and the Council rose.

div.head: SOLDIER SHOT DEAD AT BLSLEY
div.p: A SOLDIER SHOT DEAD AT BLSLEY
EXTRAORDINARY AFFRAY

An affray Whi-ch-h-aWii-iaTfatal result took place on Sunday night near the Guards' camp, Bisley, between half a dozen soldiers and a civilian named James Collyer. The latter shot Private Thomas Townsend, ot the Second Battalion Scots Guards, who has since died. Collyer was engaged at Brookwood Asylum as under gardener. He went about nine o'clock to meet his wife, who had been to chapel. On the way he met some soldiers—two belonging to the Scots Guards and the others to the Somersetshire Light Infantry. It is stated that they mistook Collyer for some other man. They struck him and knocked him about cruelly. On escaping Collyer went to his cottage and brought out a double-barrelled gun. The soldiers,on seeing him returning, said. "Here he comes • let us do for him." .They took out their knives. Collyer then shot Townsend in the stomach. The soldier fell unconscious. A fellow workman of Collyer's ran up and got the gun away from him. Collyer, who was very excited, said the soldiers wanted to kill him. Townsend died two hours afterwards. Collyer had several ribs broken and his head injured. Several of the soldiers have been placed under arrest by the Military authorities.

I,WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL AND
SOCIETIES.

In the course of an article on the above subject ,the "Liverpool Daily Post" says that the year 1875 iwas that in which' the Warrington United Trades eirtincil first saw the light. The United Trades Colin- ;cil was more the outcome of tile prevailing national sentiment then prevalent among the working men 'of the country than of any local circumstances. The strike of engineers in Newe,astle in 1871, and the support extended to them by their fellow socie- ties s had given a great impetus to the movement, ?and thus it was that the idea of forming a united 'council for all the trades in Warrington was' first •entertained. The matter was talked over at the workshops, at the workmen's homes, and 'at the different trade society meetings for some time. There was a danger, however, of the movement beginning and ending in talk, and it was only when some societies, bolder than their neighbours, took the matter up in earnest that the scheme made any appreciable advance. These societies appointed delegates to meet, not to discuss the pros. and tons., for these had been threshed longand anxiously before, but to organise the council. Accordingly, on the 113th September, 1875, there met for that purpose In a small room in the King's Arms Inn, Buttermarket- st., delegates from the File Smiths' Society (Messrs. James Rigby and J. Glieve), the glass cutters (Mather), the iron and steel wire drawers (Thomas Bosward), the boiler-makers and iron ship builders (George Venables), the White Cross Ironworks (Tinker), and the carpenters and joiners (John Bell.) Such was the humble origin of the council, but these delegates meant business, and forthwith proceeded to elect office bearers. As the delegates from the largest trade society, the iron and steel wire drawers, Mr. Bosward was very properly ' elected chairman,a position whieh he held until 1884. The other original office bearers of the council were Mr. Venables (vice-chairman) and Mr. Bell (secretary and treasurer). What really was the first meeting and com- mencement of the first quarter of the council was held on the 4th October, 1875, and at this meeting its strength was augmented by the addition of the Plasterers' Society the glass bottle makers, and brick makers. The boiler- makers and iron shipbuilders had also become affiliated. These ten societies, therefore, may justly claim the honour of having laid the foundation of a central admin- istrative board for any one or all of the local trades. The early years of the council were years of considerable difficulty, but these were met and have been partially overcome by a steadfastness of purpose worthy of such a cause. Partially ovecome only, it is true, for there yet remains considerable work to be done before the council tan be put in a position to make its power for good properly felt. Small though the beginning of the Coun- cil was, its presence in the community of trades was speedily made known. There was at that time a strike among the file makers, and a representation was made to the council at their first meeting to do something on their behalf. The council promptly raised a considerable sum, which was handed over to the strikers, and in 1876 £36 was raised for the glasscutters's strike. The accounts for the first year of the council submitted at the first annual meeting held in October, 1876, showed that there- -ceipts had been £5B 18s. oid., and expenses £5O 18s. Bd., leaving a substantial balance in hand of £7 19s. cid. Some critics condemn trades unions, and say that they encourage strikes, but this criticism, whether true or not, cannot well be applied to the Warrington Council. On the 26th September, 1877, a special meeting of the coun- cil was held for the purpose of hearing a report from the Brickmakers' Society as to receiving notice from their employers for a reduction of wages. The following reso- lution was drawn up :—" That the United Trades Council of Warrington are of opinion that, under the circum- stances of the building trade being dull and the position of Warrington with reference to society men and non- society men, and also there being bricks imported into the town at a price that the Warrington employers can- not possibly come& against, the brickmakers ought by all possible means in their power to try to come to terms without resorting to a strike by accepting the em- ployers' offer, or by having the dispute settled by arbi- tration." This shows the common sense view of things adopted by the council, and evidences their desire for , fair play on both sides. Various other strikes have en-. gaged the attention of the council, particularly the joiners' strike in 1877, the bottleinakers' dispute in 1878, the wiredrawers' strike in 1884, the glassmakers' dispute in 1885, the printers' dispute in 1886, the file glass critters' dispute in 1877, the Warrington coopers' strike, mid the Corporation ash and van men agitation in 1889. Though these and kindred subjects came most directly under the notice of the council, they by no means absorb their energies. At the various meetings of the council interesting discussions are entered into regarding the leading questions of the day, particularly their bear- ing on the working man. The Merchant Shipping Bill, the Compensation to Workmen's Bill, and the Employers' Liability Bill, in their turn, came before them, and petitions were forwarded to the borough member of Parliament. It is interesting to find what was the opinion of a body of practical working men such as composed the Warring- ton United Trades Council regarding the great depres- sion of trade in 1884. In response to a circular from the Glasgow United Trades Council inviting the Warrington Council to express an opinion on the matter, the council said that they believed the depression in trade in War- rington was owing mainly to foreign competition, and to excessive railway rates for the transit of goods. It is gratifying, also, to find the same indicators of the work- ing man's opinion say in their report for 1889 that that year had been the most prolific ef better trade and acti- vity that had been known for a number of years, and that nearly all branches of industry in the district had been fairly well employed during that year. The council also entertain the mental improvement of the working man as an object greatly to be desired, and took an active part in the early endeavours, to have the Warrington Library made entirely free, and also, in conjunction with Mr. Madeley, the librarian, and others, were active in 1888 in their endeavours to form an institution for technical instruction in Warrington. In November of last year Professor Gonner, of Liverpool, gave an interesting lecture under the aus- pices of the council in the Co-operative Hall. This lecture was an eminent success, and steps are being taken to have such lectures repeated yearly. The council is composed of delegates from the various trade societies in Warrington and vicinity, and its object is the establishment of a more intimate connection be- tween all branches of the operative classes, and giving increased efficiency to the operations of trade societies. It is, of course, a branch of the United Trades Council for the Kingdom, and regularly sends its monetary con- tribution to the Parliamentary Committee of that body. The Warrington trades—at any rate, several of them— fought shy at becoming affiliated to one central body, anif the council had frequently to make appeals to the outstanding societies for their countenance and support. Thresepeerteaivseonsoepireothaiesblyof was tchienattthesytrecnogntshidefroerd tthheeiirr, respective needs, and that they failed to look at it in the light that in one central cambination they would have a leverage by which all parties interested could command and speedily secure redress. The following societies now comprise the Warrington, Council :—The wiredrawers, wire weavers, bakers, file- smiths, ironmoulders, amalgamated engineers, steam engine makers, Dan= and Bewsey ironworkers, stone- masons, bricklayers, glass cutters, glass makers, joiners, coopers, and tanners (newly formed). In Warrington as elsewhere, the Trades Council is an acknowledged power and were all the trade societies in town to become affiliated the power would be all the greater. Union is strength, in greater union is greater strength, but in the greatest union would be the greatest strength—that would be when the employers and employes combine to protect their mutual interest, if such combination could be brought about on this side of Utopia. In April, 1889, tho Council joined the Labour Electoral Association of Great Britain and Ireland. The present meeting-place of the council is in the' Horsetnarket-at. Coffee-rooms, Warrington, where they meet on the second Tuesday of every month. at the annual meeting on the 7th October, 1884, Mr. John Grealey, of 5, Bennett-st., Warrington, was elected pre- sident, in room of Mr. Bosward, resigned. He still retains that office. Ile is a delegate from the Bakers' Society, and takes at active interest in that society and in the council. Mr. William Bullock, 10, Brackley-at., a wiredrawer at Messrs. Rylands Bros.. Limited, is the energetic secretary of the council, a post which he has held since November, 1886. He is also a member of the Wiredrawers' Society, and is one of their most active office-bearers. These two gentlemen were elected dele- gates to the trade demonstration to be held in Liverpool on the 6th of September, 1890. The article is accom- peeled by a portrait of Mr. Bullock.

div.head: REMOVAL OF MRS. MAYBRICK.
div.p: REMOVAL OF MRS. MAYBRICK.

Mrs. Maybrick is about to take up her residence in Aylesbury Goal, being moved thence from Woking. Bucks has latterly become so virtuous that its large pri- son, has internally, looked quite desolate from wants of occupants; so the Goverment authorities, availing them- selves of the power derived from the Prison Act, are sending the Bucks offenders elsewhere, and turning the old binding into a female penitentiary for the benefit of the' Country at large.

div.head: [VERDICTS OF MURDER. . •
div.p: [VERDICTS OF MURDER. . •

Thomas Gribbin, shoemaker, was on Wednesday, found guilty of the murder of a man named Kane, in whose house he lodged in the saltmarket, Glasgow. On Glasgow Fair Saturday, when both men were drunk, Gribbin attacked Kane with a knife and stabbed him seventeen titnes in the head and face and once in the chest. At an inquest in Liverpool, on Wednesday, a verdict of wilful murder was returned against Robert Lynch, who qbarrelled with his wife in a court at Tox- teth Park a few days ago, and stabbed the woman so seriously that she died.

INTERMENT OF THE BODIE3.

The funeral Of the girl Farbnond took place on Satur- day afternoon, the body being interred at Sutton church. There was no display of feeling. On Sunday afternoon the deceased girl Anders was buried in a speciaby pre- pared grave, in Burtonwood churchyard. A large num- ber of the villagers were present, and manifested their sympathy with the distressed parent. The scene was a most pathetic one, all the brothers and sisters of the deceased .showing their- grief in an unmistakeable manner.
MEEfING OF THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

_ The proceedings of the British Assoeiation gathering at Leeds commenced on Wednesday, with every prospect that there will be throughout a large attendance of members and a series of interesting meetings. The General Gommittee met in the afternoon, when the report of the Council was presented,. in 'which it was announced that Edinburgh had renewed its invitation to 'the Association of 1892. The report also showed what steps had been taken to carry out resolutions adopted last year with the object of urging the Indian Govern- ' ment to procure anthropometric •measurements of a representative series of tribes and castes, and to adopt cettain suggestions as to information which might be included in a religious census of India. The cash balance in hand was rep)rted to be nearly ENO,' and it was stated that the Association had investments valued at £12,800. In the evening the President,. (Sir Frederick Abel) delivered his opening address to a large gathering of members and associates. The address was mainly a review of the progress which has been made in the various departments of science since 1888, !ivlien the last meeting of the Association was held in Leeds. Having called the ettention to the remarkable developments in electricity, notably those in connection with the tele- graph, the telephone, and the electric light,!_l.2ir Frederick enlarged upon the importance of the application of voltaic electricity to the welding: and frsien of metals, the result of which had been to give practical value to certain substances formerly of scientific value only. In regard to the application of science to naval and military requirements, he dealt at some length with the progress which has been made in the production of smokeless powders. Experiments made in this ccuntry show that satisfactory results were attainable with more than one variety of these, and the experience of Germany afforded indications of changes itt warfare likely to result from their genera' adoption. Other subjects touched on had relation to mining clad technical educa- tion. . _

The meeting of the British Association was continued at Leeds, on Thursday, when work was commenced simultaneously in the whole.of the eight sections. The principal business of the day was the de:ivery of ad- dresses by the Presidents of sections. Professor Green in the Geological Section, devoted his address to the con- sideration of the value of geology as an educational instrumert. In the Chemical Section, the President, Professor Thorpe, in his, address dwelt on the extraordinary series of discoveries by Priestly, the I son of a Yorkshire cloth dresser, who while ministering I to a Dissenting congregation, was induced by the accident of living near a brewer' to. study the properties of carbonic acid, and thus gained for himself the title of father of pneumatic chemistry. In the Economic Science Section the keynote struck by Professor Alfred Marshall. I in his address. on competition was continued throughout the day,.several papers on kindred loonies being read and discussed. Dr. Evans's address to the Anthropological Section was read in his absence. Captain Noble&. address in the Mechanical Science Section dealt mainly with naval and military matters. In the Geographical Section Sir It Lambert Playfair discussed the physica,l and historical aspects of the Mediterranean, a region which he described as the emblem of fertility and the cradle of civilisation.

div.head: DR PARKER ON PREACHERS.
div.p: DR PARKER ON PREACHERS.

Dr. Parker is down in the provinces lecturing. In 'Newcastle he has been interviewed by a reporter of the "Leader," in reply to whose questions he made some interesting statements. The pastor of the City,- Temple considers that the prospects of the Christian pulpit in England at this. moment are far from sheering. He said: "lam requested to introduce men to eminent pulpits. but I really do. not know in what direction to turn ;for preachers. Only within the last fortnight have been asked to introduce men to two of the most conspicuous pulpits, and in answer to my inquiry for men worthy of the poskions I can only get a dreary negative. For my comfort I am told that though there are fewer out- standing preachers than there were a generation ago, yet the general average is higher. I get all the comfort I can out of the assurance but an. still left in a very dispirited condition of mind. I think preachers thenwlves may be partly to blame, for they do not suffi- ciently magnify their office. The. pulpit is dying of cowardice. We are at any rate dying of cowardice. It is decaying through homage paid to. conventionality and a mean desire to be regarded as. very definite and con- sistent. The pulpit should be larger than the nress and larger than the platform. The spirit of the age is affect- ing leading articles quite as much as it is affecting prose sermons. Hardly any man ever reads a leading article of a column long. Sermons are also being reduced to paragraphs. The new journalism is affecting the new preaching. There is at this moment a most serious defi- ciency in genuine popular pulpit power. We have got our college machines at work, and it seems to be thought necessary that we should keep them in action, no 'tatter what kind of metal they turn out. I thoroughly believe that two colleges are quite enobgh for English Congregationalism, and / should not be sorry if one of them occasionally took a rest of five years' duration. Men are not made preachers; they are predestined from all eternity to be preachers. Supposing there are 2,000 preachers in England, I think it would be a great mercy if eighteen hundred of them were never to preach again. Would I then turn these men out of the Church ? Far from it. I believe that many a man is gifted with genius quite as useful as the preacher's, but that his gift lies in a postoral rather than in a pulpit direction. Some of the most useful ministers I know are hardly second class preachers. I consider that 200 preachers would be an abundant supply for England. Why not have preaching only now and then, say once a quarter or once in six months; what in the name of reason can men want with more preaching who have been listening with both ears to sermons for more than half a century? They ought to be out teaching others and helping others. Speculation should always be balanced by service."
TETE CHARGE AGAINST THEATRICALS. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN AN EARLESTOWN

div.head: POLICE CELL.
div.p: POLICE CELL.

On Saturday, at the Newton-le-Willows Town hail, before Messrs. W. F. Gooch and T. V. Mitchell, •Arthur Armfield and his wife Lillie, described as theatrical artistes, were charged on remand with stealing two tin trunks and a quantity of wearing apparel, altogether of the value of about .£7, the property of an actress named Mildred Cohen, of 42, Thompson-st., Liverpool. It appeared that the pri- soners and the prosecutrix were members of a com- pany which occupied the boards of the Alexandra Theatre, Earlestown, in the preceding week, and lodged together at tha house of a Mrs. Waddilove, in Booth-st., Earlestown. Last Saturday week prosecu- trix journeyed to Liverpool and left the trunks containing the apparel in care of the landlady. The female prisoner subsequently informed the landlady that she was to take the boxes, and accordingly she and her husband departed with them. The female 'had informed Mrs. Waddilove that a letter addressed to them at the Bootle Post Office would find thorn, but when the prosecutrix returned on the Monday and informed the police about the matter it was ascertained that they had booked to Manchester. Poilce-constable Bowes, of Earlestown, followed them, and after visiting several theatres and places of amuse- ment, arrested them in the upper circle of St. James's Theatre. They were conveyed to Newton-le-Willows, and on Tuesday they were formally remanded until the following Saturday on a charge of stealing the trunks and the clothing. Evidence was given at cpasiderable length on Saturday, and the prosecutrix, in reply to the male prisoner, said she did not make any charge against him. In reply to a question by the wife, she admitted having lent some of the articles to the female prisoner. A second charte of attempting to commit suicide was then brought against the female prisoner. After the remand of 'the prisoners they were placed in separate cells at the Police Station. Police-Constable Bowes subsequently saw the female prisoner lying uncon- scious in her cell, and having an appearance of being almost suffocated. Ile found that she had torn a portion of her clothing into shreds, and these she had tied tightly round her neck three or four times. The strings were cut and she recovered consciousness. She after- wards said, "Why didn't you let me do it? I would rather die than bear this disgrace." The bench dismis.sed the charge against the husband, and ha was liberated, while his wife was committed to prison for fourteen days for the theft, and was committed for trial at the sessions on the charge of attempting to commit suicide.

THE Rev. FRANK BALLARD, who is a The Church and Wesleyan minister, an M.A., and!' Amusements. Bachelor of Science, is causing a stir amongst the dry bones of theology by the OP' and vigorous way in which he is dealing the question—" What are Churches For F'' three of the work, which he is writing as an wer to this important question, relates to Church's Mission of Amusement." It is publish by Mr. Elliott Stock, London, price sixpence, and is thus accessible to all who take an interest in the subject. There are not a few ministers who be- lieve with the Rev. ARCHIBALD G. BaowN that amusement is the mission of the Devil rather than of the Church; and it is Mr. BALLARD'S WIC t° combat this narrow notion. In doing so, he rushes full tilt against a large number of opponents; bUt he carries a free lance and is in no wise afraid in an encounter. He is of the new school, and Ive can well believe,that his mode of dealing with the issue has startled, and even shocked, some of the most earnest and devoted, but "older end," 01 Wesleyans. They do not forget that John \Vest once wrote :—" As we have no play-days, the school being taught every day in the Year but Sundays, so neither do we allow in3Y time for play in any day." They argue fr°lll this that WESLEY would not have shown anY interest in amusements as connected with the. Church; and perhaps they are right in their infer; ence ; but that is no proof that WESLEY ViCall; have been right. He was certainly wrong in nur: mg no provision for school children having Pa) time. His system in this respect was bad alike for health and for education; and the question is now more or less agitating the Churches is whether it is not bad to ignore " play time "—tha, is amusement—for children of larger growth. It Ist, Mr. BALLARD'S view—and in this we agree wit' him—that, as the mass of people:will and renst have amusement, the Churches should put then'. selves in touch with the people, and see to it that their amusements shall be elevating and OA degrading. He puts a broad interpretation uPe* the Apostolic injunction "As we have opportunitio let us do good unto all men." The desire for amusement, for relaxation, or recreation, after hard work, is a prompting of nature—just as is the desire for food—and it is quite as legitimate t° satisfy one want as it is to satisfy the other' But recreation is like all good things; it 0/ be used or it may be abused; and people Wil_te discuss the amusement question are not s' ways careful to distinguish between the We' The Rev. Theodore L. CUYLER is said to have remarked that "It is the mark of a babY be everlastingly crying for amusements." " lastingly" is a good word, but it is out of place 111 discussing the Church's mission of amusement' , Nobody has suggested that amusement should be "everlasting," or that it should have a first place inconsideration. The difficulty is to get it at 1171. consideration; and the result is that the Church?: losing its hold upon the world. There are lint ters who will say—" Better for the world to perdition alone than that the Church should h: dragged down with it "—pretty much as J°llo,, WESLEY might have answered if anyone had suv gested that scholars would do more work if had more play. It is a:very easy way of disposi" of the case to imply that the desire for atnust,?, ment is either childish or devilish; but people W."O- are put off in this way are apt to reflect that ever ministers are not always writing or preaching ses mons ; that some of them are known to plaY ten,lll,,e's ride bicycles, sing songs, and make thenise'_',a merry at evening parties—amongst very gu'-- people, of course. Some of them find it necessl too, like SPURGEON, to soothe themselves N°.o a cigar, or spend a month or so in the year at that, or the other seaside resort. DICK, Tog, allbe HARRY don't do these things—not because tic spirit isn't willing, but because the purse is so they have to content themselves with a Pilje e4:l nister "free-and-easy," where coarse tastes are ml to in a coarse fashion; and the search for ere. og ment ends sometimes in a fine of "five shilllotsa, and costs." Granted that this is not as it gni ei be, the question is—Are we to level up, or le,s:at down? The Rev. FRANK BALLARD belieVOS that the process should be one. of leveling UP, alicit to it is, or should be, the mission of the churcu begin that process. He would have a Reelea,tl°oo Committee in connection with every chure", oh a that provision might be made for young ancirore being well and yet innocently entertained. than that, he would endeavour to brighten beautify the lives of the masses, by giving th.ell:o such entertainments as they are partial to, bust free from the objectionable features Whi ch irt , 0 present often surround such entertainments: ect, short, believing that "religion never was desigailio , to make our pleasures less," he would seek to 01 people happy in this life,whilst preparing thorn:ray; , the happiness of the life to come. He has set n' self a difficult task in this new call to the cori verted amongst his own class; but he may console himself with the reflection that he is in the rights and that time is on his side. fut. The Fair Trade party tried a few years ago, by means which were the reverse of fair, to secure a ruling influence in the conference; but they were speedily found 'out and snuffed out. This Year it would seem that the Socialistic element has been tolerably strong; but it has not proved strong enouei to carry the Congress in favour, for instance, of Mr. J. MACDONALD'S proposal that 110 candidate should receive the support of the Working-classes unless he went in for nationalisa- tion al land, shipping, railways, and all other rneans 'of production. There can be no harm in 'raising these issues ; on the contrary they need to le discussed frankly and fully. The danger is 'that some of the leaders of the working-classes ThaY commit themselves to propositions which will tot stand the wear and tear of practical applica- tion, and which will, therefore, hinder rather than help true progress. Fortunately for the Trades 'Unionists, the Parliamentary Committee has, as a rule, been composed of cautious, far-seeing men, Who have been content to do one thing at a time and do it well. It is in this way that the legisla- tive triumphs of labour have been won; and the thanks of all workers, Unionists and non-Unionists, are due to men like Mr. BROADHU RST who, in season and out of season, have pressed the claims of labour upon the country and ur on Parliament. There was an attempt, on Tuesday, to call in ques- tion the action 'of the Parliamentary Committee with regard to an Eight Hours Bill for miners; but Mr. Ihromnreasr showed that they had done What they could on the lines laid down in previous Years, and the delegates, as awhole, approved of the eonduct of the Committee by adopting the report on the subject 'by 2158 to 92 votes. So far as miners are concerned, the question of eight hours labour may now 'be said to be ripe for settlement. It is genemllyconceded that in an arduous and danger- s underground occupation eight hours each day iS quitelong enough to work. The only issue is, 'Whether it will become necessary to enforce the eYafern by Parliamentary enactment. It is at pre- aent in 'force in some parts of the country; and if tile Miners generally could act in unison, as they teeent„ s.cted in the demand for advanced wages, re nuttter would be settled without the aid of 'egislation. But settiled it will be before long-- elle 'way or the other—and then will commence *the greater struggle which will determine whether the .eight hours system shall become the rule of /v,°rk -in other occupations. It is pretty evident, .. 'nerefere, that labour and capital have troublous itilnee to pass through ; and we may expect to a ear a good deal during the next few years 41)614 • the trade of the country being mined, and of the British ',Empire being endangered. It is the usual way of meeting, in the first instance, the.iemand of the labourer for a more equal (livision of the fruits of industry. But there is no eund for serious alarm. The capitalist 'knows 'ow to take care of himself; and the 'worker, 'When all is done and said, will get no more than his due. It is satisfactory to reflect that, 'With the tendency to unity of action on the part ef Skilled and unskilled workers, there is lessened "langer of rash and ill-considered: measures being taken. The more frade-Unionists discuss these -Matters in Congress, the better it will be in the long run for capital as well as labour.

'Factories WE have received a copy ,of the in correspondence on Indian legislation , India. which took place between "Vicount "Caoss, as Secretary of State for India, and Mr. RY H.ARRISOK, President of the Blackburn 'and District Chamber of Commerce. It 'proves beYcnd doubt, as urged in these 'columnsa few raonths ago, that the Bill for amending -the Fac- -I°l7 Act in India itself requires to be amended; Itad that being the state of the case the corres- Pondence has been wisely referred. to the Govern- Inent of India. Lord Caoss deals with the auhieet as if he knew very little about it, which is 13robahly the fact; but it is well that he recognised the -weight of the arguments which were address- 'od to him before it was too late. We figured in the Labour Congress at Berlin as 'benevolent in our factory legislation; but nothing was of co urse 'afcl of the abominably long hours which men, Wornen and children have to work in the cotton mills of 7:fridia. Medical authorities in our great ,PePendency are agreed in saying ;that the,Jong nours,and high temperature of that country are 'ruining the health ,of the factoxy workers. '!he 'Poor wretches are in no respect organised as are like classes of operatives in this country, and the 'result is that they are left to the tender mercies of 'Bombay millowncrs, which are found to be cruel. If we have found benefit from the Factory -Acts as in force at home—and who will deny that those benefits are enormous ?—why should we hesitate about enacting similar measures in India, which is equally anderthe control of the Crown? The poorer and more Cependent the 'people are, the ,greater the need for dealing fairly by them and exercising a watchful care over their interests. t °sides, to lea- 'e mattercas they are is to give an undue advantage to the sma,nufacturers ,of India he most they can claim is to be put, as to corn- Petitiomon an Nual footing with our cotton manu- facturers at home. We me certainly not called l'lson to handicap ourselves in the race, and at the E4rae time make ourselves party to the infiction of 'cruelty and irOstice upcn the down-Irodden toilers of India. The issue is ne, too, which affects W;3l"kulen of all clasces ; for so long as we permit lactories.to run absurdly long hours in India the ' chance is lessened of ,reducing the hours of labour at home. But we urge on the higher gnounds of equity and common humanity that the operatives of India shall be afforded, so far ,as the law is ;con- cerned, as ample protection as is afforded the factory workers of Lancashire and Cheshire. Lord CROSS isinvested with great power as Secretary Of State; let him see to it that he ,exercises that Power in the iuterests &lire of Luria and of Eng- land.

HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT.

CROSBY S; WALKER-S.. TO THE PUBLIC. On WEDNESDAY, September 3rd, we shall CLOSE OUR ESTABLISHMENT AT ONE O'CLOCK, and Every Wednes- day in each week till further notice. The Half-Holiday Movement was originated by our assistants and received our approval. At a meeting of employers at the Albion Hotel it was decided by a majority to close each week, if the closing was unanimous. Some of the leading drapers (to their shame be it said) opposed the idea, and were the cause of the move- ment falling through. The Executive Committee have, how- ever, by their energy, left no stone unturned in order to bring about the desired result. The consequence is that in the suburbs, and outside the principal streets of the city, the shopkeepers all close at one o'clock every Wednesday, thus putting to the blush (if ever they do blush) the large traders of the city who should have led the way instead of follow- ing. We have received from the Committees of various districts Copies of Resolutions passed at their meetings, from which we quote as follows:

August 18th, 1890. Harpurhey, Rochdale-road, Queen's-road, and District Half-holiday Movement. Gentlemen,—You may be aware that a movement has been on foot for some time to obtain a weekly half-holiday by closing all shops one half-day per week, and in this district the matter has been taken up with such unanimity that practically the whole district have approved of it. We com- menced to close on August 13. The question whether or not the arrangement can be successfully continued depends very much upon large and influential places of business, as those who close will hardly continue doing so with the centre of the city doing business as usual. Therefore, we, as a committee, consisting of seventeen, and representing grocers, drapers, bootmakers, furniture dealers, Scc., in the above districts, respectfully ask you to consider the matter, and show that your firm, at any rate, will not stand in the , way of this beneficial reform.--Signed on behalf of Com- mittee,
HENRY NOBLE. Chairman. ,FRED.OODEN,.Hon. Secretary:

99, Droylsden-road, Newton Hett-h. To Crosby and Walker's. LADIES OF MANCHESTER AND ELSEWHERE We call upon you for your co-operation and kindly assist- ance. Without you drapers might close their shops and seek some other means of gaining a livelihood ; without your aid this movement will fall through. Will you let it fall through? Many of you have sons and daughters in the business. Let your answer be an emphatic NO I _ HOW CAN YOU HELP US?

By purchasing ;-forel-One—O.'e-loCk--oTt Wednesdays, or on some other day in the week, but above all by refusing to patronise the grasping, greedy, avaricious shopkeepers who will not close their establishments. If ladies will only come to the rescue and show that they approve of this movement by declining to purchase from the mean drapers who persist in keeping open, they will soon compel them to close. DO THEY REQUIRE A HOLIDAY? Artisans, warehousemen, bank clerks, 34c., have their weekly half-holiday ; and why not the drapers' assistants ? Drapers' assistants work long hours ; though their work is not laborious, it is tedious. A draper's assistant must dress well, have a good appearance, be cheerful, courteous, patient, chatty with customers, must have artistic taste in the blend- ing of colours and arrangement of goods (as the attractive drapers' windows in every large town testifies), and lastly, he must possess the genius of a diplomatist and the patience of Job to succeed in pleasing every customer. Surely such med require a half-holiday as much as our labouring classes, ann much more so than the bank clerk, who commences at ten and finishes at four.

For many years the drapers' assistants have struggled to procure this much desired half-holiday, and have only par- tially succeeded. Once again the movement is brought to the front, not aggressively or noisily, but in a calm rational manner that merits the attention and considel.ation of the public. Once again the movement is threatened with a com- plete overthrow. We have, however,eonsented to step into the breach, and to close, whether any one follows our example or not, as the movement has our sympathy. We shall be pleased to receive any letters on the subject, either for or against the movement.
NOTE.-WE CLOSE ON WEDNESDAYS AT ONE O'CLOCK, COMMENCING WEDNESDAY, SEPT. 3RD.

When 'Warrington people go away into strange places, such as Llandudno, for instance, they go in for enjoyment in a style that is sometimes the ad- miration of the natives. I heard the other day of a party of exclirsionists, not wholly unconnected with the licensed trade that is so freely represented in Warrington, who trusted themselves on hoard the St. Tudno. The journey was made in safety, but to one of the party, at least, the perils of the sea were as nothing to the perils of the dinner table. What fine writers speak of as a " recherch6 spread," was, of course, one of the features of the trip. The fish and soup had been successfully sampled, and the more substantial joints and vege- tables were being manipulateal, when the hero of the occasion noticed some fine apricots resting on a plate within reach. Transferring one to his plate, he was boon afterwards heard to observe that "that turmot " was sweet, and although a neigh- bour persuaded him to "try a little butter with it," he is still of the opinion that Llandudno tur- nips are of a remarkably peculiar sort.

Speaking of humours of the dinner table recalls an anecdote yet related in Warrington with regard to a citizen who was occupied in filling up at a '"swell feed." "Give us some more of that her- ring, please," he observed to a water, at the same time indicating the salmon. The waiter was so much knocked back that he forgot his usual stolid- ity, and exclaimed " That, sir, is salmon; and it cost 3s. a pound." It was the turn of the diner to be a bit staggered, but he was equal to the occas- sion. "I don't care what it cost, but it's rare and good," was the reply, and he had another helping. There was another little incident, too. When the waiter passed a plate containing toothpicks to an- other of the feasters,he was observed to look con- siderably perturbed, and made, answer "No, thanks, lad; I've tried two or three of 'em, and don't care about 'ern." Poor fellow; at that par- ticular moment they were sticking somewhere in the region of his ribs.

When imagination gets a start in Warrington, the mole-hill soon becomes a mountain. The other Saturday evening an old man named Welsh was knocked down by a trap in Horsemarket-st. It was freely tallced about town for the next two or three days that the occupants of the trap were driving at something like lightning speed, and in consequence of complaints the police had scarcely any option but to issue a summons against the driver. When the matter was sifted, and cold facts had to be dealt with, the case was dismissed by the magistrates on Monday. I only mention the case as a means of drawing attention to the pig-beaded 'way in which people persist in planting themselves at Market-gate like so many automatic sweatmeat machines, to the great annoyance of foot passengers as well as carriage folk, and to the no small danger of themselves. There is generally a regular crowd there on Saturday nights, and the poor policemen who happen to be 'on that beat are harassed almost out of their wits in endeavouring Ito keep the 'thoroughfare clear. One of the wit- nesses in this particular case admitted that when the accident occurred he himself had been stand- ing at Market-gate for a matter of a couple of hours. lam naturally a kind sort of chap, but couldn't complain if some of these persistent obstructionists were occasionally to receive a gentle push from some equine proboscis—not sufficient to hurt them, but just enough to frighten them a bit.

How ongthing suggests another. Referring to Market-gate brings to mind an incident that occurred in •Sankey-at. on Wednesday night. Of late there have been all kinds of labour strikes up • and clown the country, and locally there has been some talk of an alleged police strike—in embyro. -Matters of this kind seem to be infectious, and a certain 'bus 'horse detailed on the Sankey Bridges -route, on 'Wednesday night took it into its 'head to get up a little strike on its own account. 'Having imbibed the latest principles as to hours Of work, 'the intelligent 'quadruped, after due •reflection on the matter, resolved to strike. And straightway it did strike. The 'bus was 'standing in the shadow tf Trinity Church, and 'had got its complement of passengers. The, driver gave the regulation gee-up " signal. 'Did that horse move? It 'budged not an inch: baCk was up," so to speak, and moreavor it was on strike. You could-scarcely say that it was "out" on strike, because it was in the shafts, and could not, ,so to put it, hand in its uniform, but it did strike all the same. The fight lasted for some time, but the public gave in their verdict against the striker, and putting their shoulders to the wheels of the 'bus literally forced the malcontent , on its unwilling Way. The 'crowd then cheered 'thel result, and for the present the 'bus-horse s'trike'is, " eff." It'seerns to me that the horse made a • mistake in acting altogether on it own responsibi- lity. It Should have called a meeting in the stables for the purposes of combination, far if each horse on day had struck at the same time 'some- thing might have come of it.

The Sunday Sacred Coricezts that are to be herd in the Public Hall during 'the winter, indicate a move in the right direction. Warrington is evi- dentiy on the improve. We have had bands in the Park occasionally on Sundays during the so- called summer season, which is passing away like an empty dream, and now we are to have Sunday concerts. Of course, we Shall have to pay for them, and why 'not? Its a great reflection on the piiblic that they have not contributed more generously to the band fund, but in the ease of the concerts s small charge will be made for admission. If we go on like this we shall have the Museum and the go Room open on Sun- day neat. The way is being cleared for pro- gress in the direction of making Sunday a daron which the toilers can find enjoyment and recrea- tion in -a way that will make the Sabbath some- thing different to them than the present dull and listless °" day of rest." The first concert will be given tomorrow (Sunday) evening, and as it does • not commence until 8.15, it will Tot interfere With 'the attendance of church and chapel goers. The frst concert will inelude "Gems from Elijah,' nd will no doubt prove a draw.

THE REMOVAL POF DEAD ;BODIES : &Ma ITLAIt POINT.

A point affecting the removal of dead bodies, and in reference to Which considerable doubt,exists in the min& of a large number 4of people, W/18 raised at the dose of an inquest 1-.;eld by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner for South-west :Lanca- shire, at Illaydock, on Monde.y afternoon: The ' deceased was a collier who, after meeting with an aceident,died whilst being convesied to the hospital. Hedley, the Government Inspector of Mines, , remarked to the deputy-coroner that there had been some disagreement in reference to the disposal of the body. He asked him to say what should be done in the ease of a man dying on the road— whether he should be taken home orremoved to the ' nearest public-house.---The Deputy-Coroner said the first thing to be done was to give information to the police, and then the body ought to be taken to the nearest convenient place. It should not be removed out of the township, and as he understood that Mr. Robinson, the manager, gave instructions for the body to be removed to the Rams Head Hotel, he considered that was quite right. He did not like to say anything more, but it was natural that the selatives should want the body removed to some particular place.. Under the circumstances before them, however, it would have been wrong to have allowed it. The best plan when anything of the kind happened was to let the police know at once, and they would soon put matters right. A MAN SUFFOCATED AT A WIDNES WORKS. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner,,on Thursday, afternoon held an inquest upon the body Of Jas. Bright, a chemical labourer, 53 years of age, who had resided at 13,'Victoria-rd., , who was suffocated in a•boiler at the, Widnes Alkali 'Works, on Tuesday ,afternoon.—The 'works-were repro:ented by Mr. Thillough,fthe engineer, and Mr. HammiL, minager,—Joseph Bnght,ll.s years of age, said he was .engaged with his father in cleaning a , boiler at the works on Tuesday morning. About half- past eleven a man,named Jones was -" gassed,' and had to be asSisted out 42 the boiler. Attwelve O'elock witness went todtEnner, and when he returned at aluarter to one, he found his sfather lying at the bottom of the beiler,,qulte dead- The boiler was connected with a sewer by,means of .fin iron pipe and the gas drom the sewer entered the boiler. They pulled the cotton waste out of the -" go-off tap" about eleven o'clock, in order that the water might ,be taken away to the sewer, while they were scaling the inside of the boiler. On account of the heat, they could not stop in the boiler longer than ten or fifteenminutes.—William Jones, fitter, said he went into the boiler to clean the steam gauge at the far end, when sometbing like dust blew in his face.and he was suffocated. He bad to be assisted out and taken home. Witness pulled the cotton waste out of the tap. He had beenemployed in this kind of work for many years. He warned the deceased last week not to work with the gas tap ,open. The deceased, in reply, said witness was too careful. The deceased was a practical man. He had never known the "blow off tap" open before last week.—Mr. Hammill said the sewer referred to I was Mowers Brook.—John Wesley Harrison said he as- stinted to carry deceased from the boiler. There was a ' smell of gas at the time.—Tbomss Gibson, foreman fitter, said in sweeping and scaling the boiler there would be a quantity of dust, but he had never „experienced any gas.—The jury retired to consider their verdict and after ten minutes absence, the foreman (Mr. James Hurrows), said the jury were not satisfied as to whether dust or gas suffocated the deceased. They thought the foreman of the boilers was to blame in-not seeing that the sewer pipes were plugged up.—Mr. Palm: We think the firm to 'blame. —The repret atative3 of the firm undertook that when any person went into the boiler, the junctions should be stopped up, so as to prevent any connection between the boiler and the sewer. The jury then re- turned a verdict of accidental death.

, PLEURO-PNEUMONIA AT Rom. Pleuro-pneumonia, which was ,discovered to have broken out about a week ago at Old Hall Farm, Bold, occupied by Mr. William Johnson, continues to spread. The cow which Mr. Johnson purchased from Mr. Bennet, cattle dealer, of Padgate, in February last, has been slaughtered, and on Wednesday ten other head of cattle on the same farm were destroyed. On Thursday, seven cows belonging to Mr. Thomas Baker, whose farm is adjacent to Mr. Johnson's, were also slaughtered, as they had come in contact with the infected beasts. BATHS, all kinds.—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington. Branoh—Barlestown.—Advt.

. - STABBING A GIRL AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Miskeler, a youth, of Barn-st., was charged with having wounded a girl named Mary Jane Reilly, by stabbing her in the back, on the 23rd August. It was alleged that the prisorer and Reilly had a quarrel in Sankey-st., and on separa- ting the fatter went down an entry. The prisoner pur- sued her, and stabbed her in the back just below the shoulder blade. Reilly, who was very much excited, did not feel the wound very much at the time,and several hours afterwards she was locked up for being drunk and disorderly. When in the cell she was found to be bleed- ing very much from the wound, and she was placed in chair of Dr. O'Keeffe. The prisoner waS committed for trial, bail being allowed. UMBRELLAS RE.COVERED at the shortest notice.-3. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. SMART CAPTURE BY 4. WIDNES POLICEMAN. Patrick Goulding and John Davies, of no fixed abode, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday, charged with stealing a firkin of butter, worth £3, the property of Francis Lawrenson, grocer, Victoria-rd. While on duty in Victoria-rd., on Saturday, P.C. Thomp- son saw the prisoners carrying the firkin of butter through an entry behind Lacey-st. He followed them, and in answer to his questions they said they had got the butter from Liverpool and it belonged to themselves. He took Goulding into custody, Davies making his escape, and it being discovered that the butter had been stolen from Mr. Lawrenson's shop, Davies was apprehended in a lodging-house. The prisoners were remanded for a week so that inquiries might be made into their antecedents. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DOTTores Sankey-st.. Warrington.—.Advt.

div.head: NATIONAL MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: NATIONAL MEETING AT WIDNES.

Under the auspices of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League a meeting was held in the Drill Hall, on Tuesday night. A charge was made for admission and there was a fair attendance. Dr. O'Keeffe presided and he was supported by Mr. D. Unity M.P., the Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Clark. Messrs R. Carey, T. Snape, J. Morrison, F. Rartland, and H. B. Shores. Letters of apology for non-attendance had been sent by Mr. 11. Wade Dea- con, Alderman Muspratt. and Mr. T. S. Timmis.— Mr. Carey moved and Mn. Morrison seconded the following resolution "That we emphatically condemn the unheard of tyrany of the coercion and shadowing regime of Mr. Balfour, in Ireland, and that we are re- joiced to see how ineffectual it is to break the unconquer- able spirit of the Irish people ; and that it also gives us satisfaction to see that the narrow-minded and outrage- ous policy is recoiling upon the heads of the present Government, as the bye elections which have taken Plsre in this country so forcibly show."—Mr. Brume sup- norted the resolution which was carried unanimously.— A 'vote of confidence was passed in the Irish Parliament- ary party and Mr. Crilly made a speech in reply. At the conclusion of the meeting a banquet was held at the Alexandra Hotel.
