The finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £653 Us. 11d. on general fund, and £l,OOO on loan account. The following accounts were recommended for payment; general fund, £271 9s. sd. ; and loan account, £lB7 13s. 100 There

was still a balance of £602 Os. 7d. to be collected on General District Rate. NUISANCE mamma. Mr. Dobson moved that Mr. J. Percival be appointed inspector of nuisances for the district comprised within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852, for a term of one year, at a salary after the rate of £125 a year, and that the approval of the Local .Government Board be obtained to such appointment. Carried

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Canon Wood pre- sided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, A. Salkeld, J. J. Howitt, G. Moss (clerk.) FORMATION OF AN ART cuss. At a meeting of the School Management Committee held on August 19th, it was recommended: That Mr. T. Cook, of Northwich, be allowed the use of a class-room at Greenway-road school at the nominal fee of is. for the purpose of holding an Art Class during the ensuing winter, on condition that he admits elementary school teachers to the class at half the usual cost. That the salary of Miss A. M. Kilburn head teacher at Greenway- road girls school, be advanced to £lOO per annum dating from October let next.—That the salary of Miss A. Price assistant teacher at the Greenway-road girls school be advanced to £5O per annum dating from October Ist next.—Mr. Howitt moved and Dr. McDougall seconded the adoption of the report.—The Chairman said while it was an admirable thing; that there should be art teaching in the town he did not know whether it was wise for the Board to lettheir rooms be used for a private enterprise in which the gentleman would make some profit, unless he paid the expenses the Board would incur.—The Clerk said the cost of coal and gas for the class would be £1 ls.—Dr. McDougall said tl.O Stipula- tion as to pupil teachers saved considerably more than that sum, and the Board had made an exceed- ingly good bargain both in the interests of pupil teachers as well as assisiant masters who required art training. Mr. Howitt said he was the instigator of Mr. Cook coin- ing to Runcorn. Mr. Cook was certainly not the servant of the Board in the same way as a school teacher, but he took the whole of the responsibility of the art classes and all he asked for was the accommodation of a room. He did not ask for it for nothing but they had offcred it to him. In other towns the School Board had had to spend large sums in forming art set-idols, and he thought the Board had made a good bargain.—Mr. Taylor hoped there would be no obstacles thrown in the way of the proposal. If they had to take the 'matter up themselves, it would cost about £3OO. The class would be a very great help to the teachers of the School Board and a great advantage to the town.—The Chairman said as the matter was such a small one, it could only be tried, and he shoulel not offer any further opposition.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: DOMESTIC ECONOIff AND DRILL.
div.p: DOMESTIC ECONOIff AND DRILL.

At a meeting of the School Management Committee on the 22nd August, it was recommended That Domestic Economy be taught at Greenway-road Girls Schools, to the higher standard. A memorandum from the Head Master at the Greenway-road Boys School was read, sug- gesting the desirability of teaching drill to the upper standard boys. The Clerk was instructed to make some inquiries on the subject and report to a future meeting. —Mr. Howitt, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the head teacher asked to be allowed to teach domes- tic economy. When their teachers suggested such things all honours was due to them.—Carried.
THE EXAMINITIONS.-.AN EVENINQ SCHOOL TO BE FORMED.

Ai a meeting of the School Management Committee on the 27th August, A.M. Inspector's reports of the examinations at the Board Schools were read, and on the whole were considered highly satisfactory. The follow- ing are extracts from the reports :—Mill Brow Infant's School: This school is now doing exceedingly well. Merit grant, excellent. Total grant per head 175., amounting to £96 is. Greenway-rd. Schools: This School is on very good order and on the whole does ex- ceedingly well. Per centage of passes 94. Merit grant excellent. Total grant 20s. 4d. (This is the second year in succession that the school has obtained the distinction of excellent). Girls: The girls are in very good order, the work generally is good., and shows a marked improve- ment on last years' resetts. Percentage of passes 93 ; merit grant, good, total grant per head 18s. 3d. The amount of grant earned by the two schools £442 18s. Bd., but a deduction of £ll3 Ss. 2d. is made under article 114 which limits the amount payable to £l7s. ed. per head of the average attendance. The question of opening an evening school was considered and a draft scheme was submitted by Mr. Hewitt. In order to give the proposal fair trial, it was recommended that an evening school be opened at Greenway-rd. Board School in the last week of September next, and carried on during the winter if a sufficient number •of pupils present themselves. That the following strojects be taught, viz., reading, writ- ing, arithmetic, English, algebra, euclid, men- suration, also Shorthand, chemistry, and French, if classes in these subjects can be formed. That Mr. J. F. Moulton, bethe head master and that assistants arid teachers of special subject&be appointed as may be found necessary immediately after the school is opened, at zilch rates of salary as the Board may then determine. —Dr. Gastaldi moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Howitt seconded, and said the fact that two of the schools has taken excellent, and the other school good, was a groat feather in the cap of Runcorn School Board. A great deal df the success was due to the admirable staff ef teacloers and he proposed that a letter of congra- tulation be sent to the head teachers. In reply to a remark by the chairman, Mr. Howitt said he had avoided mixing rap any other school in the matter. He should be happy if every school in Runcorn obtained excellent, but he objected to any school master, or school managers putting it forth in the public newspapers that they bad taken eXCatent " when they had not done so. Let then , in all hnnelty be fair and above board.—Dr. Gastalai : Wmed you tiouht it if you saw it in the newspapers,that my schodl had passed 98 per cent.—Mr. Hewitt : I claret thin'k anything is itnpossiliie for the Catholic Schools Dr. McDougall referred with gratification to the eecel- lent reports obtained, but threrg lit it would be unwise that theletter proposed should he sent. He suggested that the opinion ;of the Board be entered upon the minutes instead. The n'iinutes werc passed and the docter's suggestion adapted.

div.head: ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.

The annual election ef five members of Ituaeorn Board of 'lmprovement Commissioners took place on 'Thur.*lay. There were nine candidates for the five eeats,..and greatet interest was taken in the contest than for several years past. Three of the retiring members, Messrs. Taylor, Whittaker, and Fisher, together with "Messrs. Thomas Handley and Waiter Timmins, issued a joint address. asking for the support of the ratepayers on the ground of past cervices of the retiring members, and the ability of the group. 4' The rapid growth of our town" the sdffiressproneeded, "‘which we believe will con- tinue and increase as the result of the completion Of the Ship Ga,nal, must bring to the front the provision of 'a pleasure-or recreation ground, a proposal which has our warmest-sympathy, .and to which we shall give our earnest attention, as weare confident that a practical scheme for utilizing the common lands for the purpose can'he carried out with a minimum of expense to the ratepavers, and be of incalculable benefit to the inhabi- tants:" The other eandidates, Messrs. P. Smith, S. Tarwood, R. Abel, and E. Wynne-Humph- reys, came 'forward independent of each other, and issued separate addresses. Mr. Yarwood drew attention to the fact that he had been a reSident of the town for4o years and was thoroughly conversant With the requirements of the district. His general policy would be to promote and maintain effici- ency without extravagance in all departments.—Mr. R. , Abel, in his address, said he believed that the opening of the Ship Canal for traffic would further develop the resources of Runcorn and bring into its midst new and important industries which would require to be dealt with ima liberal spirit by the Commissioners. Whilst refraining from making mail promises, impracticable of fulfilment, he promised, if elected, to zealously watch the interests of the inhabitants and to give every attention to all questions affecting town improvements, its sanita- tion and recreation, with due regard to efficiency and economy.. Mr. Smith besides issuing addresses, explained his views more fully by means of public meetings. A crowd of nearly 300 persons assembled at the Market Square, on Wednesday evening to hear Mr. Smith expound his views. A man named Mr. Jones volunteered to conduct the meeting., and after he had delivered a brief address, Mr. Smith said they were told that they had no works list now but they had got another one, and he advised the ratepayers to choose the best men as their representa- tives irrespective of any religious or political feeling. Get men who would represent them, and whom they could approach and tell their grievances too. He mixed more amongst working-men than any other member of the Board of Commiesioners (applause) and they could say to him "Hello, Peter, there is such a thing wants doing" and he endeavoured without making a great nlise at the Board meetings to get the officials to put it right in an 4 agreeable and commonsense fashion. It was the first time that a retiring member had been left off the. list when there had been one issued, but he had been left off without even being asked whether he was willing to stand ("Shame") and he could only think that the list issued was an attempt at dictation. After a reference to the other candidates, Mr. Smith said three years ago the working classes got it into their heads that he in- tended to give public baths if returned. No i•easorable man would expect him to do so and he never said he should. He said he should advocate public baths, and he had done so to the best of his ability, but one man amongst 18 could not have his own way. It was the majority that ruled, and he could not get a majority in favour of public baths, because of the cost. It was sug- gested that Mr. Brunner ought to give them baths, but he said let them start amongst themselves and he offered to give £2OO if the remainder of the sum required was forthcoming in three or four months. (Applause.) He urged the ratepayers to break up this new clique , , which had been formed; and if they thought him ' ; worthy give him a vote as an independent candidate. Did they ever know him do a dishonourable action or not express his opinion like a man. Why at the Board

meeting that day, some members wanted to ashphalte Higher Runcorn. Be objected and said flags were good enough. (Hear, hear.) They com- pared the road to Bold - street, Liverpool, (laughter.) He and Mr. unison inquired the cost of the ashpnalte and one of the officials said" I don't know." Then it was stated to be only an experiment, and he told them to make the experiment in the centre of the town, where there was plenty of traffic and people could see now it acted. They were doing all they could for Higher Runcorn, but in other parts of the town, Dukes Field for instance, they had to jump to get over the high road, and then very likely they would drop into a pool of water. (Applause) He and Mr. Imison succeeded in having the recommendation referred back, and it was for the ratepayers to say, by their votes, whether their money had to be spent in making a nice soft carpet of ashphalte for the Higher Runcorn people. (Applause.) He concluded by asking those present to plump for him. Mr. Humphreys held a meeting in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Wednesday night and there was a capital attendance of the public. Mr. J. Jeffspresided, and said all the public roads in the town appeared to managed by a clique, and he was supporting Mr. Humphreys because he was an independent man. He had been paying rates for 18 years, and he failed to see what improvements the Com- missioners had carried out. They said" Look at Waterloo Bridge " and he said "Look at it." (Laughter and ap- plause.) Mr. Jeffs spoke in favour of baths and a pleasure ground.—Mr. Humphreys at the outset referred to the magic address which bore the signature of five gentlemen. A few years ago there WU a works list—a black list, which the electors had to swallow whether they would or not. They had been told that time WAS passed, but from information he had received he feared there was a danger of those times returning. Desiring to enlist the sympathy of the working-men in his cancildature, he went to one of the largest works in the town ; but he was told he could not be allowed in the works; that there would be no canvas- sing there, and that what was denied to him would be denied to every other candidate. What was the result? That very day two of the gentlemen who had signed that address had been in Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works distributing their literature. (Shame.) Unless this pri- vilege was accorded to each of the candidates he must conclude that despite protestations to the contrary, the great works of the town were not standing on one side in this matter. (Applahse.) He asked those present to give him the benefit of their votes as a protest against such conduct. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Humphreys declared himself in favour of public baths, and until it was proved to him by figures that the cost would be too great a burden on the rates, he should bring the question forward. He advocated the adoption of the Ballot Act in their local elections and the division of the town into wards. He desired the abolition of the resi- dential qualification for Commissioners,and said a recre- ation ground was a necessity. He should strongly recommend the acquisition of the common lands, which he believed could be obtained on fairly good terms as a recreation ground. He desired to offer further facilities to the Free Library, which the Commissioners could do by the grant of a building, and the money now paid in rent could be used in the purchase of books Which were needed. (Hear, hear.) Referring to his connection with the Musical Society and the Extension Lectures, Mr. Humphreys said the manner in which he had conducted those movements was a fair argument that he should dis- play the same energy as a Commissioner. If returned he would endeavour to fulfil every pledge he had made. (Applause.) He moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mr. Stanway seconded, and described how the men from the works were formerly led to the poll like sheep to the slaughter. He hoped the ratepayers would plump for the independent men. The poll opened at nine o'clock in the market hall. Mr. J. W. Lightburn was the returning officer, and he was assisted the Law Clerk (Mr. Lake) and a staff of officials. There was very little excitement, and voting proceeded quietly. The pcll was closed at four o'clock and half-an-hour later the result was declared as follows : S. Taylor 468 W. Timmins 326 It. Abel 448 W. Whittaker P. Smith 363 T. Handley E. W. Humphreys 360 IS. Yarwood 266 W. Fisher 350 The first five are elected. Mr. Humphreys moved a vote of thanks to the returning officer. His experience of the election that day had made him more determined than ever to endeavour to change the system. (Hear, hear.) He said the place had been a bear garden the whole of the day.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion and said the election had been conducted in a manner that no one could raise the least objection to. (Hear, hear). He thank- ed the ratepayers for again placing him on the Board. He would endeavour in the future as in the past, to con- duct the business of the Board, in the same manner he managed his own office. (Applause). Mr. Abel also re- turned his thahks to the ratepayers, and said he would do his utmost for the interests of the town.—Mr. Smith in his speech, said he still believed baths a necessity, and he should like to have the opinion of Mr. Abel on the question. While rejocing that the list had been broken, he regretted that Mr. Whittaker, who had served the town for so many years had been defeated.—The motion was carried. Mr. Lightburn, in reply, said the election had been carried out in an impartial manner and in accordance with the Act of Parliament.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. H. SINGLETON, OF WIDNES.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. H. SINGLETON, OF WIDNES.

A marriage in which great interest was taken was celebrated at St. Francis Xavier's, Liverpool, on Tuesday afternoon, :the contracting parties being Mr. Harry Singleton, butcher, Victoria-road,Widnes, eldest son of the late Mr. John Singleton, of Widnes, and Miss Lizzie Moysey, second daughter of Mr. Win. Movsey, of BrunswiCk-road, Liverpool. The officiating clergymen were the Rev. Father Gerrard, assisted by the Rev. Father Rimmer, of Widnes. The bride was led to the altar and given away by her father, and she was charmingly attired in a dress of grey surah, trimmed with white crepe de chine, with a tulle veil, and a wreath of orange blossom. She also carried a bouquet of rare orchids and other choice white flowers, the gift of the bridegroom. The brides- maids were Miss Moysey and Miss Theresa Moysey (sisters of the bride), Miss Marrow (cousin of the bride), and Miss Wright (cousin of the bride-groom.) They wore beautiful costumes of grey cloth, stylishly trimmed with white pointed lace. They also wore hats to match, trimmed with plumes of white feathers, and each carried a bouquet of white flowers and wore a gold horse shoe bangle, the gifts of the bridgep,r)om. The duties of best man were discharged by Mr. T. Singleton, and the following gentlemen were the groomsmen -- Messrs. Gar Kiddie, E. Tallm, and J. •Pearson. The service having been gone through and the register duly attested, the wedding party were conveyed in ten equipages to Derby Hall, where the wedding breakfast was served, and various forms of amusement were i indulged in until evening, when a ball was given in honour of the occasion. The happy pair after re4!eiving the sincere congratulations of their many friends, left Liverpool by the 10.5 p.m. train for Dublin via Holybead,where the honeymoon will be spent. The presents were numerous and valuable.

div.head: TRIP FROM STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: TRIP FROM STOCKTON HEATH.

On Thursday an excursion from Stockton Heath took place to Beaumaris, and Menai Straits. The train conveying the party left the Central station at 8,50, arriving in Liverpool 2.15, thus giving the excursionists the opportunity of a brief stay in Liverpool, which was taken advantage of in view- ing some of the principal sights of the City, and likewise getting light refreshments before leaving the landing stage by the St. Tudno at 10.30. The weather,which had been wet and threatening in the early morning,and had prevented some from going, now gave way to a bright and sunny day. The party arrived in Llandudno about 12.50, highly delighted with their beautiful voyage. When the St. Tudno was about two miles outside Llan- dudno Bay, a most exciting scene was witnessed both by the large number of passengers on board, and the hun clreds who were on the pier, waiting the arrival of the two steamers, which arrive here about the same time from Liverpool, viz., the St. Tudno and the old com- pany's boat, Bonnie Princess which loaves Liverpool three qwters of an hour before the St. Tudno. As every minute the St. Tudno was gaining on the Bonnie Princess it became the matter of anxious speculation which boat would gain the pier first, and no doubt many bets were lost and won during the last quarter of an hour. When about half a mile from the pier the St. Tudno came abreast of the Bonnie Princess, and appa- rently not more than eight or ten yards away from her Now the excitement on both boats, and by the visitors on the pier, became keener and keener, but by the swift progress and skilful handling- of his boat the captain brought the St. Tudno to the pier just before the Bonnie Princess could get there. On landing the party got sub- stantial refreShments,after which some strolled round'the town,some went on towards Conway;the scene of the late boating fatality, some went on the Great Ormes Head, and others visited the Hippy Valley. This Valley has been presented to the town by Lord Mostyn, and a beau- tiful drinking fountain has just been built which will be a great boon to the thousands who wander round and through its beahtifully laid out grounds. Others of the party went on to Beaumaris, Bangnr, and Menai Straits, arid enjoyed this additional trip immensely. The return journey back from Llandudno began at four o'clock, and Liverpool was reached about 6.30. After a stroll round Liverpool, and a visit to some of the places of interest, the party arrived back in Warrington in good time, and all highly delighted with their day's out.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."- Amongst the subjects that will engage the atten- tion of IVidnes Local Board on Tuesday will be that of technical education. A proposal was made at the last meeting to adopt the Technical Education Act, but the majority of the members were not con- versant in the provisions of the Act, and others vi,._•re deterred with doubt by the fact that an ex.pendi- .ture could be incurred each year equal to a penny in the .e. A suggestion that a grant of about £lOO or .£2OO should be made to the Science and Art School appeared to meet with considerable favour and as there is a fear that this idea may be adopted, it should be pointed out that all the legislation of the present time discountenances the granting of money by public authorities for purposes over which they have no control. Taxation without represen- tation is tyranny. The payment of a grant to a private school would not be a just tax upon the ratepayers. • At the same time the importance of technical education is very great, and in a town like Widnes, whose industries are of a very intricate and techni- cal character, it is a necessity. The question is how can that education be the most cheaply and efficiently provided for the rising generation. In the opinion of the writer it is by adopting the Act in its entirety as originally proposed by the General Purposes Committee. and in also adopting the suggestion of Dr. O'Keeffe, and placing the con- trol of the Act under a Committee of the School Board, together with an equzil number of members of the Local Board. The School Board are in the best position for efficiently and cheaply carrying on 'the work. They have three commodious and admirably fitted up schools in the town and a staff of masters capable of teaching many of the subjects needed. The School Board are at the present time consid- ering how best they can introduce manual instruc- tion into the curriculum of the schools, and this is a very important branch( of technical education. The manual instruction is to be (a) in the use of ordin- ary tools used in handicrafts in wood or iron; (b) given out of school hours in a properly fitted work- shop; and (c) work must be done from drawings to scale previously made by the students. If it ap- pears that the school is properly provided with plant for instruction and that the teaching is fairly good, a grant of 6s. or if excellent of 7s. will be made by Government for any scholar instructed provided that he has passed the fourth standard; that he has received manual instruction for at least two hours a week for 22 weeks during the school year and that each scholar has attended the day school with reasonable regularity. Everyone must recognise that a boy so educated is much better equipped for hM start in life than is at present the case, and it is to be hoped the 'School Board will be enabled to make the requisite arrangements. The Market Hall is at present a comparatively useless structure and could be turned into an admirable workshop for the boys with con- siderable advantage to the people of the town. How would the Local Board receive such a propos- al from the School Board men if made. There would be no loss of revenue. • The proceedings of the Runcorn School Board, on Tuesday evening, were full of interest. It was re- ported that the schools under the Board's control had passed the ordeal of the Government inspec- tion in a highly creditable manner, two having earned the " excellent " grant, and a third was des- cribed as good. Then, principally through the in- strumentality of Mr. Howitt, an art class will be conducted at Greenway-road School during the com- ing winter by Mr. Cook, of Northwich, and to en- courage him in his labours, the Board are allowing him the use of a room at the nominal rent of is. They have, however, obtained a most important concession—that pupil teachers shall be permitted to attend the class for half the usual fee—which, it was justly argued, was ample compensation for the nominal rent. The Board have also decided to com- mence evening classes, at which there will be taught the three R's, mensuration, algebra, English,French, chemistry, and shorthand -that is, if sufficient pupils put in an appearance. It was quite time that somening in this directien was attempted,and it is to be -hoped that the youth of the town will ap- preciate the effort which is being made in their be- half, and will enrol themselves as students in suffi- cient numbers to ensure the continuance of the classes. There seems to be an epidemic of violence at Widnes at the present time, kicking,bottle throwing,. and stabbing is very prevalent, and the magistrates have had a very busy time of it during the past six weeks. In every instance the assaults have been committed under the influence of drink—What are- our teetotal missionaries doing? Pointsmen on the railways usually embellish their • cabins with a few plants, but there is one of the tribe who occupies the Duke's cabin between Run- corn Docks and Weston Point, who outstrips them all. In his very small rude lee hut, he has growing between thirty and forty pleas of various descrip- tions and the place presents the appearance of a greenhouse. But the pride of the pointsman is a tomato tree, set in a box which occupies a corner of the hut, and the bows are now bent down with the delightful fruit, which is. not yet ripe. A second tomato tree also bears fruit, but for want of soil, it is stunted of growth. Pictures from the best Illus- trated papers adorn the walls where there are no plants, and the cabin is "as clean as a new pin." Scores of those out for it constitutional, call upon the pointsman to view his bright display of foliage", of which he is justly proud.
BREWSTER SESSETNS AT NEWTON.

The annual licensing sessions for the Newton-le-- Willows Petty Sessional Division were held at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Saturday, when the magistrates on the bench were Mr. W. Mitchell (in the chair) and Mr. T. D. Grimke.

div.head: SUPERINTENDENT WEIR'S REPORT.
div.p: SUPERINTENDENT WEIR'S REPORT.

Superintendent Weir submitted the following report in regard to the Warrington portion of the Division : " I have the honour to submit a ten years' compara- tive return of the persons licensed to sell intoxicating liquor within my part of your division. The return also shows the proceedings taken for drunkenness within the same period, and it will be observed that this year's proceedings show an increase of eighteen on the pre- ceding year. The number of persons applying for renewal of their licenses is one less than last year, viz : 46 licensed `victuallers, 16 beersellers on, nine beer off, and one wine or spirit grocer. One licensed victualler has been convicted of permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises, the license being transferred to another person. There is only one new application for a license. It is that of James Jackson, of the "Crown and Cushion Inn" beerhouse, Penketh, who applies for a wine license,. in addition to the beer license which he now holds. William Attfield (Gilbey's agent), who holds a license for the sale of wines and spirits, in Queen-st., Earlestown, has notified me that it is his intention to add the adjoin- ing shop (which has become empty) to his licensed pre- mises for better accommodation. I have no objection to such addition, but have told Mr. Attfield to wait and obtain your sanction at the Licensing Session." Attached to the report was a comparative return for the last ten years, showing that in 1681 there were 48 licensed vic- tuallers, in 1890, 46: beerhouse keepers, 1881, 15; 1890, 16- off-licenses, 1881. 12 ; 1890, 1; total number of licenses, 1881, 77; 1890, 72; convicted of offences against their licenses, 1881, 6; 1890, 1; persons pro- ceeded against for drunkenness, 1881, 201; 1890, 231. The existing licenses in this portion of the division were renewed, there being no objections made. SMERTIT4NDENT MAMMON'S MPORT. . . .

Superintendent'Brassington reported that in the town. ships of Goßoerne and Haydock,which formed the Wigan portion of the division, there were 13 innkeepers, 1 spirit grocer, and 18 beersellers, being one more innkeeper and one less beerseller than in the previous year. There had been 154- persons proceeded against for drunkenness, be- ing an incrgase of 19. During the year one becrseller had been twice convicted, and had since left the pre- mises. The Railway Hotel. Golborne, and the Huntsman Inn, Haydock, for which provisional grants of licenses to sell all intoxicating liquors were granted at the last ses- sions, had been completed, and were now tenanted. Both were commodious and substantial buildings, and had replaced old and unsuitable licensed houses. The houses generally had been well conducted, and be had no objection to the renewal of any of the licOnses. The num- ber of persons proceeded against for all kinds of offences was 302. against 316 in 1889.—The existing licenses were renewed.

THE APPLICATIONS. Mr. William Attfield, wine and spirit dealer, -queen- street, Earlestown, applied for sanction to proposed alterations to his premises by the addition of an adjoin- ing shop. Superintendent Weir said he had no objection to the application, and the Bench remarked that it would be granted.—Mr. John 0. Swift (St. Helens), applied, on behalf of James Jackson, of the Crown and Cushion Inn, Penketh, for a wine license, in addition to the beer license held by him and also for sanction to make addi- tions and structural alterations to his licensed premises by the addition of an adjoining cottage. Mr. Swift stated that the applicant had occupied the Crown and Cushion Inn for about 15 years, and during the whole of that time there had been no complaint against him. The inn was the terminus for the 'buses from Warrington, and wine was often called for.—Superintendent Weir, in answer to the Bench, said he had no objection, and he thought the alterations were necessary. The applica- tion was granted. This concluded the business of the sessions,

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DRIN'S AND THEFT.

Thomas Clark, Shin Canal labourer, was brought up in custody on a charge of having stolen a vest,value fis. from the shop-door of Edgar Valentine Morton, pawn- broker, Bridge-foot. When apprehended prisoner was under the influence of liquor, and afterwards said that he should nct have taken the vest had he not been drunk. The magistrates fined him 20s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment, with hard labour.

A DISHONEST LODGER. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, a man named William Flanders was charged with having stolen a cotton jacket, value 25., the property of Sarah Payne, of Manchester-road, Rixton. He had been lodging at the house of the prosecutrix,and it was alleged that he took the jacket away with him. When appre- hended, he was wearing the jacket. He now said that he had been drinking, and did not know what he had done. The magistrates sent him to prison for 21 days, with hard labour.

div.head: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA OUTBIIEMS.
div.p: THE PLEURO-PNEUMONIA OUTBIIEMS.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, Mr. It. Pillungton was summoned for having on the 18th ult, removed a calf out of a pleuro-pneumonia infected area, without having a license authorising him to do so. It was explained that the defendant's servant obtained a license for the animal to be brought into the borough of Warrington, which is also an infected area, but failed to procure one allowing of its removal out of the other area. Superintendent Weir said that he be- lieved Mr. Pilkington intended to comply with the law, and under the circumstances a fine of is. and costs only was imposed. WARRINGTON.ROUGHS AND NEW POLICEMEN.

• Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a young rough named Micl.ael Cunningham made his thirteenth appearance. The charges against him were drunkenness, disorderly conduct, and assault, P.C. Har- rington deposing that prisoner struck and kicked him while on the way to the Bridewell. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that prisoner never worked, and was in the habit et molesting new policemen. If he could not do it alone, he got others to help him. A policeman with a good stick—one of the olden times—would have had a lad like him in hand, without troubling the magistrates. Prisoner was sent to jail for three months, with hard labour.

div.head: ALLEGED FIIRIOLTS DRIVLNG.
div.p: ALLEGED FIIRIOLTS DRIVLNG.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Henry Brown, landlord of the Coffee House, Horse- market-st., was summoned for furiously driving a horse and trap in that street on Saturday night, the 25th ult. It was given in evidence that about 7.30 on the night in question the defendant was seen to drive through Market-gate slowly towards his residence. As he ap- proached it, it was alleged, the, speed was accelerated. AS an old man was crossing the street the trap caught him, the wheel passing over his neck and the side of the head. The man, whose name was Walsh, was conveyed in the trap to the Infirmary, where he remained in an unconscious condition for 48 hours afterwards. Mr. Jenkins, who represented the defendant, called evidence to the effect that defendant exercised due care and cau- tion. There was no intention to drive furiously. The old man appeared to be confused by the people calling to him "Mind the trap !" The Bench held that the evi- dence was not sufficiently strong to justify them in re- cording a conviction' and dismissed the case.—Mr. Jenkins, on behalf of the defendant, said that all possible kindness would he shown towards the injured man.— youth, named James Taylor, was summoned for driving a horse and spring cart furiously in Sankey-st., on Sun- day evening, the 24th ult. The defendant, whe stated that he was endeavouring to catch a train, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days in default.—For a similar offence in Bridge-st., on Monday evening, a youth named Samuel Sutcliffe was also fined 10s. and costs.

Secretaries of Cricket Cluts are requested to note that reports of matches rlayed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON V. RusHomm—The return match was played at Arpley on Saturday, and resulted in an easy win for the home team, who were without Mr. S. M. Crosfield. Mr. J. J. Crosfield, who was captain, on winning the toss, took Lawton to the wicket with him, and faced the deliveries of Holme and Ibbotson. Play ruled close for some time, Crosfield being the first to retire. Lawton left at 25. Clarke and Dickson made a good stand, and took the score to 56 before Clarke was bowled for 23, which included three Cs. Armstrong was at the wicket a long time for his 2, when he wag given out lbw, 4 for 68. Jolley and Yonge were both beaten at 85. Voisev assisted to raise the score to 106, when he was well taken in the slips. R. Dickson was next out fora well-played 54, which included seven 4's. one 3, six 2's and singles. He went in first wicket down and was out eighth. Reynolds showed a little of his old form, and put on 20, the innings closing for 141. Rusholme sent McNiven and Farrington to bat, the at- tack being byJolley and Crosfield. Maidens were the order at the start, and before a run bad been scored, Farrington was out. Colson gave two chances imme- diately, but succeeded in scoring one, when he was clean bowled by Jolley, 2 for 1. McNiveh scored 5, when he was taken by Lawton, who had gone on in place of Crosfield, 3 for 9. Merry was bowled next ball 4 for 9, and Holden taken next over off Jolley, half of the wickets being down for 9. With one run added, McArley hit wicket, while at 11 Wadsworth was stumped and Holden run out. Leeming was the only man who played the game ;be hit out vigorously and scored 20 not out, out of 32. THE EXAMINER,: BATURDAT; SEPTEMBER 6, 1890.
TRADES UNION CONGRESS AT LIVER
POOL.

The 23rd annual Trades Union Congress opened in Hope Hall, Liverpool, on Monday. lit is just fifteen ;years since the congress met in Liverpool, and this second visit haa created unusual interest and excitement among the trades unionists of that city. The present congress is, in some respects, the most remarkable that has been held since the Labour Parliament commenced its annual meetings. In the fleet place, the delegates who assembled ire the hall exceeded by over 936 the num- ber ordinarily gathered at these conferences. The con- gress in previous years has generally consisted of not more than about gOOl delegates. On Monielity• • 250 soeieties and trade councils were represented hy, some- thing lie 450 delegates- and it is expected that befOre the sittings are concluded this number will be farther augmented. Then, agelie: for the first rime in the !theory of the congress, unskilled: tabour sent it representatie,es to take part in the deliberations, whila the sreteral women's anions, which have been formed during the past year, were also no without their spokeswomen, there being at least a dozen' lady delegates pesent on behalf of the bookbinders,. the upholsterer% the matter- makers, and the laundresses.. Business was commenced a few minutes after noon, wilier the chair was taken by Mr. J. Swift, of Manchester,.by virtue of hie. position err chairman of the Parliameethry Committee: Then by the unanimousconsent of the-meeting, Mr. W. Matkin of Liverpool, was elected presidentof the corpess, and the same unanimity was displayed in the appoint- ment of vice-president, treasurer and zecretary. An unpleasant incident occurred'clusing part oil the pro- ceedings. Mr. .Tohn Williams, offflonelon, was proposing ; a Mr. Parnell, also of London, as a candidate-for the :Standing Orders Committee, when her was requested by :the chairman to leave the hall, as-he had not produced his proper credentials. There was an awkward pause alter this Unusual request, but Sir: Williams, having re- covered his breath, explained that Iliewa.s the accredited representative of the AmaigamatedSecirty of Firewood Chtters. For some reason or other,- this announcement was received with laughter, which caused another dele- gate to indignantly exclaim that a "Drowned cutteiewas as much a man as an engineer." Thechainnan them de- sired to proceed with the election of tit*. Committee, .but Mr. Williams protested against this, as a slur had been castopon him, and the applause which' followed indi- ,cated that the congress was with the aggrieved delegate. It was then explained by the chairman that the Parlia- mentary Committee had refused credentials to Mr. It it- liams,.and they were under the impression that the re- presentative of the Firewood Cutters ma that gentle- , man. That appeared not to be the case, and the matter might now be considered to be at an endl This, how, ever,: did not satisfy several of the delegates, andi Mr: Tohn Burns asked that a fulfar tioni might be given. Another delegate expressed the opinion that the explanation already offered warsufffcient, but as the congress was evidently very much divided, the difficulty was solved by accepting Mk. Williams's nomination, and referring the personal matter to the Standing Orders Committee- to report. Theother business consisted of the adoption of a resolu- tion expressing sympathy with, and promising, monetary assiStance to the strikers in Australia, the introduction of the new president, and the reading of the Parliament. ary Cbminittee's report by Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P. It had been arranged that this should conclude the day's work,, but when the President announced that the Con- gress would now adjourn till the morning, Me. Quelch, one of the" new unionists," rose and proposed that the delegates should sit till five o'clock, and not lhave the important-work before them merely in order to accept the invitation of the Mayor of Liverpool to a trip on the the river and to a conversazione at the Town MAI after- wards. The proposal was received with marked signs of dissatisfaction, and Mr. Quelch was heard with undisguised manifestations of impatience, and though his resolution found a seconder, it was, on a division, rejected by a crushing majority, only 31 delegates out of the whole body of 450 voting in its favour. The congress then adjourned.

TUESDAY. The delegates to the Trades' Union Congress reassem- bled oriTuesday morning, in Hope Hall, Liverpool/under the presidency of Mr. Matkin, who, in his inaugural address,welimmed the congress to the city, and said the development of labour within the past two years had practiealty made its previous record a matter of ancient history. Obviously the future r was for labour, and it was the duty of the congress to make increasingly pos- sible an ideal labour state, where equal opportunsties would tie open to all. The congress then proceeded to the consideration of the Parliamentary Committee's report, which was pre. sented on the previous day. As :an amendment to its adoption, M. Woods (Wigan) moved a resolution of pro- test against the action of the Committee in neglecting to carry out the instructions of the Dundee congress as to the drawingmp of an Eight Hours' Bill for miners. Mr. Cower(Durham) seconded the amendment, which was warmlysupported by Mr. Pickard, M.P., and others in the course of a prolonged and animated discussion. Mr. Broadhurst warmly defended the action of ,the Com- mittee, in referring to the Miners' Eight Hours' Bill to the only, man on that body who had practical exper- ience of 'coal mining. After a warm passage at arms between him and some of the supporters of the amend- ment, it was decided that the discussion should cease, and the amendment was then put and rejected by 258 to 92.
the evening a large numbar of the delegates and their wives were entertained to tea in the Reform Club, Dale-st.

CURE GHOST CRAZE IN GERMANY. 111 OMNI MA Berlin paper tells a strange story. The children of a school in Friedenstrasse have lately been so excited by ghost stories that even during school hours they imagined they saw fiery men, death's-heads, and the like. At ten o'clock a few mornings ago, work was beginning, when suddenly a child in the second girl's class, held in one of the upper stories, who was sitting at an open window, began to stream, crying out, " Help ! help! the Dead Hand is strangling me!" Withtart listening try her teacher, the flighted girl, who was twelve years old, rushed out of the mom, followed by.. her companions, screaming. Presently boys and girls by hundreds stumbled and fell down the stairs. Most fortunatetY none were seriously hurt, but Borneo( them had to be carried home in a fainting state. The policemen of the district deposed that the girl at the window must have been startled by a curtain which a gust of wind blew into her face.

Mr. J. Inglis (Glasgow) moved the following resolu- tion, which was seconded 1w Mr. G. J. Davies (Man- chester), and adopted :—" This congress emphatically re-affirms its previous declaration, that no measure of legislation on this question will be satisfactory to the industrial classes in this country whicu does not abolish the law of common employment; to prohibit the privi- lege hitherto enjoyed by employers to contract out of their liability and to have removed all limitation or restriction relative to the amount of compensation worli, men may be entitled to, and the Parliamentary Commit- tee are hereby instructed to introduce a Bill embracing the foregoing?'

div.head: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.-A SCENE. _ _
div.p: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.-A SCENE. _ _

Mr. E. Flarford (Cardiff) moved the resolu— tion :—" That this congress is of opinion that a much larger representation of labour in the House of Commons by men drawn from the ranks of the workmen is both desirable and necessary, and( therefore, urges all trades and industries to use their utmost efforts to give practi- cal effect toNsuch representation." (Applause.) A West Ham delegate seconded the motion. Mr. Threlfall (Southport)l, who complained that the resolution was not• advanced enough„proposed the following amendment "That this-oongress condemns the State barriers to coo— stitutional equality in parliarnentary and local represen-- tation, which prevents the industrial community from exercising the full force of its political ,rights, and which linats its freedom of choice in the selec— tion of candidates, and that the Parliamentary Cosnt, mittee be instructed to give urgency to the question withl an earnesbatterapt to bring about as soon as possible a i joint conference of all associations of a kindred nature; and that such conference be directed to devise the best methods of enacting (1) a law tor the payment of mem- bers of Parlianzent—(applause) •' (2) returning officers' charges, B:c., to be borne by the public funds, and (3) to place the election of local government boards and boards of guardians on a popular basis, and generally to assist local and national labour movements. (Applause.)— Mr. G. D. Kelley (Manchester) seconded the amend- ment, wnich, he said, if passed, would be the means of creating a National Labour Party, which was what they required .—(Applause.)--After some further discussion, the amendment was accepted, and it was agreed that it should follow the resolution.—Mr. MacDonald (London), who spoke amid continuous Interruption, moved the following amendment to the now substantive resolution; —" And that this congress declares that no candidate shallreceive the support of the working classes, toeless he declares in favour of the nationalization of land— (laughter)—shipping, railways, and all other means of prodnetion."—(Laughter.)—Mr. John Burns seoonded the amendment which was, however, lost by E. 6 against 263. The resolution was then carried by 249 voles to one.. The congress adjourned. WEDNESDAY.

The Trade Unions Congress resumed its sitttings Liverpool, on Wednesday. It was decided to accept the invitation of the Belgian Workmen's Partv to take part in the International Congress at Brussels next year, Resolutions were adopted condemning the present system of enforcing factory and workshop disciplinary fines, urging the need for the appointment of additional factory inspectors, and instructing the Parliamentary Committee to take steps to secure the payment of tho++ cognised rate of• wages to all workmen engaged+ on Government and all other works of a public charaoter. It was decided to reintroduce into Parliament a bill pro- , viding for the examination and granting of certificates of ability to men charged with the contra) of steam engines and boilers, who frequently held the lives a others. largely dependent upon them. The Congress further [ expressed the opinion that the tires had come for the abolition of the property qualification for appointment, to the magistarial bench. A series of resolutions having reference to the grievances under which seamen suffer were also adopted, and the establishment of boards of conciliation in labour disputes was approved. • THURSDAY. VOTE IN FAVOUR OF THE E/ORT FIOtTICS. DAY.

_ The most important feature of Thursday's programme at the Trades Union Congress in Liverpool„ was a dis- cussion lasting for several hours, on the question of an eight hours working day. Mr. Marks, of London, moved a resolution advocating the aid of Parliament in obtain- ing the eight hours day, while an amendment was sub- mitted by Mr. Patterson, of Durham, affirming that the best method of attaining their object was through the individual efforts of the trade societies. A somewhat heated debate followed, in the course of which the supporters of Ms. Marks held that while tinades unionism could do a great deal it could not accomplish everything, and, therefore, it would be folly not to call in the assistance of Parliament to co. ' operate with them. Mr. Abraham, M.P.,Rhondda, took this view, while Mr. Renwick, M.P., thought it would be better on economic grounds to trust to trade societies. Mr. John Burns argued that the eight hours day could only be obtained either by legislation or a general strike, which might lead to civil war, but this question did not Justify that. The amendment was lost by 181 to 173, the original resolution being carried by 193, to 1.55, In

He referred to the demand for increased facilities throughout the princi; ,pality, and' commended the eagerness with which the; people availed themselves of those facilities when offered:: Tis Lordship spoke of agriculture as a, subject not to be neglected in any system of technical instruction. Arch- deacon Farrar alsaaddressed the gathering, which was very large and'enthusiastic. Prizes were awarded in the course of therdayforperrnillion singing and other accomu-1 plishments. The President.l for the day,the•Bishop of Bangor, delivered an address, in which he said that that annual gathering served the purpose of a Sbeial' Science Congress for the principality, and tended to the intellectual advancement of the people' by festering albve for literature and music. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The cricket at old Trafford on Saturday was watched with keen interest oy several thousand persons, although the play was—as could only be expected after the recent weather generally speaking slow. A draw seemed probable until Mold knocked down three of the Notts wickets in quick succession—a proceeding which had a very great effect in securing for Lancashire a victory by 68 runs, and at the same time the second place in the first-class counties record.

In an article on the cricket season just coming to a close, the "Star" says our opinion, the Shrews- bury style of play is 'doing its best to demoralise Dig- lish cricket. Caution carried to excess is defeating its own ends. Shrewsbury's season, which began so bril- liantly, has had a lamentable finish, and the superb bs- man, starting with the essentially vicious course of play- ing first of all for safety, has fallen into a nervous, jerky, and timid mannerism, painful to all true lovers of the game. Gunn, following his chief, is little better, though every now and then, as in the famous finish be- tween M.C.C. and Australia at Lords, he reverted to lis best form with the most brilliant results. But let these two level-headed professionals take pattern by an older, and in our opinion, a more finished cricketer even than they. "The Doctor" is not so sure as he was. On a wet wicket, his play is often risky, and his hitting is up- pish. But "W. G." has the true sportsman's love of fight, and though his freedom with the bat may spoil his average, it is still true that in his happy moments there is no greater master of the game than the genial giant whom the people love, because he tries to give them "something for their money." So let the Notts cracks look to their laurels. Three Scottons in an eleven arc enough.

But, on the whole, it is not the batting which has proved to be the characteristic of the season of 1890. It has been a bowler's year. It was bowling which kept Surrey at the head of the counties. It was Martin's bowling which gave gent the third place. It was the want of reliable first-class bowling which ruined the chances of Sussex, spoiled Middlesex, and kept Glouce.s- tershire down during the early part of the summer. Had the wickets been more uniformly dry and true, we should doubtless have had an entirely different distribution of honours. As it is. players like Martin, Sharpe, Loh- man°, Attewell, Mold, Shacklock, Briggs, Peel and Wat- son are the heroes of the season in a much‘more real sense than Shrewsbury. Gunn, Grace, Webbe, and Stod- dart, while mere colts like young Hearne or Needham, or boys like Mr. Streatfeild, have every now, and then exercised a commanding influence on the fate of match- es.

Finally, there is every reason to congratulate cricketers on the rule enabling •captains to declare an innings closed. It has saved the cricketing- season of 1890 from the reproach of barrenness,, and has greatly enriched the tactics of the game. The rule as to "I b w "is still subject to abuse by some distinguished players, and it might be strengthened still further in the interests of sound cricket. A redistribution of classes, in eonnties is only fair in face of some results of tber year's play. Somersetshire's unbroken record of victory should at once have been acknowledged by her admission within the circle of first-class counties. But under the new rule she will have no chance of ranking as a fltsst-elass county till 1893. That is grossly unfair. Why should the first- class counties be rigidly confined to eight 2- Why should not the number be extended to ten, and the last t-vo moved annually blackward and forward according to their merit?

div.head: One more point. Among the younger cricketers is there a man whose all-round play promises a successor to "W. G. ? " Perhaps one—George•Lohmann.

CYCL/NG.

In the 24 hours' cycling race of the North Road Club on Saturday the records for both bicycles and tricycles were broken. M. A Holbein, the well-known long-dis- tance rider, covered 3381 miles on a bicycle, this being, 12 miles better than the previous record : and Bidlake on a tricycle did 289 miles thus beating by nine miles 052 - best performance previously.

div.head: _FOOTBALL.
div.p: _FOOTBALL.

_ The Warrington F.C. open their popular list of fixtures next week with a match on their own ground against Lancaster. Following on that, the next week there will be a still more taking engagement with Swinton. The list of fixtures includes most of the old clubs who have usually figured on the Warrington card, though some of the organisations whichhave degenerated of late in their playing capacity have been dropped off, to make place for more famous teams. Amongst the additions are I Rochdale St. Clements, Hartlepool Rovers (holders of the Durham County Cup), and a trio of well-known Welsh clubs—Llanelly, Penartk and Penygraig—the 'away" matches with whom will be taken "on tour."

Massey, the popular three-quarter, will captain the " wirepullers " this year, and as it is understood nearly all the old players are again available the team will pro- bably be coMposed pretty much as last year. There is every reason to expect that the Warringtonians will come out of the season's campaign with a good record behind them.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, on Friday. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Houghton, W. Houghton, R. Ileaton, S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sepliton ( medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector). THE Bouotion Ilir.r..—The CLERK said he had obtained copies of the new Bill of the Warrington Corporation, in which there was a clause for compensation to that Authority. He had waited on the Town Clerk, and told him that he (Mr. Sutton) would propose to that Autho- rity that the Town Clerk, himself, the Authority's sur- veyor, and the borough surveyor, should meet and en- deavour to come to an equitable arrangement. The Authority had expended moneys for sewerage.—The Su VEYOR : Our annual payments will cease, and the Cor- poration will have to take the loans over.—The Clerk's suggestion was agreed to. THE ESTIMATES.—The Clerk submitted his estimates for the coming half-year. The total sum required to be raised was £ll3 Os. 2d., and it was 'stated that id. in the £ would be sufficient to raise the sum. BIRTHS AND DEATHS.—The Medical Officer reported that there had during the month been 44 births and 20 ' deaths. The death-rate was equal to 14.7 per 1,000, as compared with 12.9 in the last three months, and 14.8 in the corresponding month last year. DEFECTIVE WATER SUPPLIES.—A letter from the Local Government Board was read in which the receipt of the Medical Officer's report was acknowledged, and it was also inquired what steps the authority proposed to take in respect to the defective water supply in Cuerdlev, Burtonwood, and Orford. The surveyor was directed to make a report on the subject.

div.head: WATtRINOTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WATtRINOTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

An extraordinary general meeting of the members Of the Warrington Musical Society was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Bold-street, on Wednes- day evening, to take into consideration, and receive a report upon, a proposed amalgamation of the society with the Orpheus Orchestral Society. Mr. John White was voted to the chair, and there was a good attendance of members. THE SOCIETY'S HISTORY. The CHAIRMAN said that the meeting was to take into I consideration certain recommendations drawn up by a sub-committee appointed at the general meeting a few weeks ago. The Musical Society had had a somewhat • chequered history, it having been all they could do to make both ends meet, and they got into low water sometimes. Although for many years they had to be content with holding miscellaneous concerts, still they kept their heads above water until Lord Cross, then Mr. Cross, came to reside near Warrington. Heseemed to put new spirit into musical matters, and resuscitated the old I Choral Society. During the period of 22 years when they had the as4istance of Dr. Hiles they had had periodical attacks of debt. Friends when appealed to had come to their assistance, largely on the understanding that they • should not get into the same position again. They had now arrived at a time when the debt was bigger than ever before. They had arrived at a great crisis in the condition of the society, and it appeared to him that the suggestions they had made were the only ones that could be carried out with a view of continuing the society. They would all be sorry that such an ancient institution as the society, should be discontinued. The first thing they had to suggest was that they must dispense with the services of an experienced and 'expensive conductor. Dr. Hiles had brought them to high state of perfection, but as far as re- karded the financial position of affairs there was much to be desired. However valuable Dr. Hiles had been in the past, and might be in the future, it was totally impossible toclear the society from debt if they were to have his experience. It appeared to the sub- Committee that if they were to carry on the society at all they must have the services of an honorary conductor,or at all events, one who resided in the place and who could give his services at a less figure than Dr. lliles could give his. (Applause.) Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, the hon. secretary, next read letters from absent members regretting inability to at- tend. Mi. Henry Roberts agreed with the sub-Com- mittee's proposals for the future management of the society, with the exception that he thought Mr. Cross- ley should not be allowed to give Ins professional services for nothing. As the conductorship of the society was a professional engagement, it should be paid for. He should be glad to see Mr. Crossley occupy the position of con- ductor.—Dr. Gornall agreed with the proposals of the sub-Committee with the exception of accepting Mr. Crossley's services free. There was too great a tendency, he thought, on the part of the public to expect honor- ary services from the professions. Mr. Crossley should be adequately paid.—Miss Clark, Lowton, strongly objected to Dr. Hiles' services being dispensed with.— Three members wrote intimating their intention to cease subscribing to the society. THE SUR-COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

The report of the Sub-Committee as to the proposed Amalgamation with. the Orpheu's Society, which was signed by Messrs. John Rylands; John White. L. W. Reynolds, J. P. Reynolds, W. Parkinson, and W. H. J. Jenkins, was read by the Hon. Sec. It recommended as follows :-1. That the advantages of the Amalgamation appear to be:—(a.) The avoidance of opposition in musical matters which would be the inevitable result of the existence in the town of two societies having similar ' objects, but acting independently. (b.) The acquisition of a capable and well-established Amateur Bard by the Musical Society, and the benefit of arrangements already made by the Orchestral Society's Committee for the, coming season (e.) The participation by the Orches- tral Society in the benefits existing under the Organ Trust Deed, and the agreement with the Public Hall Co., and also from the Musical Society's connection and ' Subscription List. (d.) The greater scope for useful work opened out by such amalgamation. 2.—That the Amalgamated Societies be called "The Warrington Medea). Society." 3.—That a special effort be made with a view to paving off a portion of the existing debt for the Musical Society, and that the balance be a charge upon surplus funds of the Amalgamated Society. 4. That all surplus funds at the end of any season shall be ap- plicable to the reductionof the above mentioned balance of debt, and to such other purposes -is the joint committee shall deem advisable. s.—That a special vote of thanks be accorded to Dr. Hiles for the services he has rendered to the Musical Societe during the past 25 years, with an expression of regret that the present financial condition of the Society will not admit of his services being retained. 6.—That Mr. Frank 11. Crossley be asked to accept the conductorship of the amalgamated Society for one year without remuneration. 7.-=That Mr. W. E. Atkin (Secretary of the Orchestral Society) be asked to act as Joint Secretary with another gentleman to he ap- pointed. B.—That the amalgamated Society give four concerts during the season, of the following nature :-1. Oratorio. 2. Other Choral Works. 3. Miscellaneous, with choruses and part songs. 4. Orchestral, with solo vocalist., 9.—That subscriptions for the four concerts be as under, or an equivalent :—Reserved seats 15s. each. Centre gallery 10s. 6d. each. 10.—That a Committee and officers be elected, fairly representing the two Societies. The SECRIZTARY said that all the members of the band had not received the report of the sub-committee, simply because he was unable to obtain their addresses. He as told by Mr. Peter Caldwell that they all knew of the matter, and that it was unnecessary to send them circu- lars.-'-Mr. J. F....sem-rise considered that the members of the hand should have had notice, and he moved that the meeting be adjourned until they, had been served with spotices.—The CHAItrMAN said it was unfortunate that the hand had not received notices, but it certainly was not tbe fault of their Secretary. Ile wished to point-out, however, that if they. (Mar( 01" carryinst out. of ,ttaa amalgamation of the societies there would he no time to make arrangements for the season, and the Society's operations would .have to be suspended for the year. The Orpheus Snciety had made their arrangements, and he theu,c,,ht it would be a great mistake if a decision was not arrived at that evening.—Mr. Eittomnsv mid under the circumstances he would withdraw the motion. CONSIDERING THE REPORT. The report was then considered, and it was at once agreed that it was advisabl. that the amalgamation should take place. Clause three, relating to liquidation of the debt, occasioned some discussion, Mr. G. Woods and others thinking that a specified sum should be named as being the amount to be wiped off by the old Society's efforts, previous to the Societies amalgamating. —The CHAIRMAN said that the sub-committee could not bind themselves to wipe off the debt, they could only make a suggestion as to it, or part of it, being wiped off. —Mr. Atkins, hon. secretary of the Orpheus Society. read a resolution of that society passed at a meeting held on the 21st. August; in reference to Clause three. The solution s;ated "that it should not be thought

unreasonable on the part of the members to expect the Musical Society to liquidate as large a portion of the debt as possible before amalgamation." Mr. Atkins mentioned that the Orpheus Society wore free from debt.—Mr. George Woods thought that the practical members should give what they could, if appealed to, and others would follow with their aid. It was a prac- tital question,and must be dealt within a practical way. , —Mr. JENKINS : Then why don't you begin it P—Mr. Woons : I have begun. I don't want to blow my own trumpet, but I have given what I can.—lt was pointed out that the Society had an organ, and that its assets were greater than its liabilities, so that it was not a bankrupt society.—Mr. L. W. REYNOLDS, hon. treasurer, said, however, that under the trust deed if the organ was sold the proceeds must go to a charitable institution and could not be used to clear off a debt. Eventually it was decided that the words" it being understood that at least half the debt be liquidated before the amalgation of the two societies" he added to clause three.—Mr. Atkins stated that this would satisfy the members of the Orpheus Society, and the, proceedings terminated.

WORKING-MEN'S MEEIING AT WARRINGTON. ADDRESS BY MR. J. WILSON, M.P. On Wednesday evening a meeting of Warrington workmen was held, under the auspices of the Warrington Trades Council, in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street. The chief speaker was Mr. J. Wilson, M.P., who gave an address on the subject —"Why should working-men be Trade Unionists?" There was a very large attendance, the hall being crowded. Mr. J. Crowther presided, and there were also on the platform, in addition to Mr. Wilson, Mr. Jamieson ( member of the executive of the Durham ' Miners' Association), Mr. B. Hall, Mr. J. Chnmes, Mr. T. Houghton, Mr. W. Gregson, Mr. H. Kent, Mr. J.Graley, and Mr. W. Bullock (secretary of the

Warrington Trades Council.) The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said the Trades ' Council had taken advantage of the fact that the Con- .ress was being held this week in Liverpool to invite Mr. ilson to come and address that meeting,. (Hear, hear.) While he was there it was nothing but fair to congratu- late Mr. Wilson upon his success so recently in his Parlia- mentary campaign in Mid-Durham. (Applause.) They were all aware that Mr. Wilson was one of the very small minority of labour members who held seats in the House of Commons. His own feeling was that as the borough franchise had now been extended some 22 years it was time that workingmen had more than eight or nine representatives in the House of Commons. (flear, hear and applause.) He had, however, every reason to believe that before long they would be better represented than they had been in the past. (Applause.) Mr. JAMIESON, in a short address, said the reason he became a trade unionist was that he was dissatisfied with the conditions of his labour. He had too many hours to work for one thing, and he had two little wage for it for another. In his employment as a miner in Durham trade unionism had shortened the hours of lads from 15 or 16 a day to 10 and 11, and those of coal-hewers from 11 and 12 to six and seven a day, and wages had at the same time been increased. (Applause.) Those were reasons why they workingmen should be trade unionists. (Hear, hear.) They not only wanted trade unionism, hut they wanted federation, and he did not think any man could be a true trade unionist who opposed federation.
gress \VP-

(Hear, hear, and applause.) _ _ Mr. J. WILSON, M.P., was received with loud applause. He remarked they workingmen would never be able to attain the object they all wished unless they identified themselves closely with each other and showed themselves eager and earnest and continuous in striving for that object. There was a newer element arising, and which, he must say, he was willing to welcome, who in the full flush of their trade unionism were going to outstrip the _ _

old men who must take a sort of corner—a super- annuated corner in an asylum. (Laughter.) He was not the man to bo wedded to any institution or cause or system, simply because he had been identified with it. He believed that institutions and systems should be laid aside as soon as they had completed their Dart. (Hear, hear.) If it could be showed:that the old trades unionism had played its part, and that the newer trades unionism had got features the older had not, then like wise men 1 they should let others carry out the work to a greater I success. (Hear, hear.) The old trades unionism of this country had a record, and the men who had written it had no reason to be ashamed of it. They had a record in the light of English history, in the homes that had been made happy, in the better condition .s of the working men, and in higher wages, which it would take the new trades unionism all its time to amend. (Hear, hear). If the same progress be made in the next 25 years that had been made in the last, the lot of the working-man would indeedbe brighter and better. There were con- tinually arising young men who could not realize the changes that had been made, and they looked with coldness and indifference upon anything that was said to point out those changes simply because it had not taken place in their day. There were lots of young men who knew the Union hut did not know the Union's work (Hear, hear). He had worked as a lad fourteen and fifteen hours a day, never seeing daylight except on [ Sundays, and then being too sleepy to look at it. ' (Hear, hear and laughter). Now, the hours of the pit - lads in Durham were not sixteen but ten, and. he might

now say, that, after negotiations with their empl-oy- ers, they had an offer from the latter that would still further shorten the hours of 15,000 men and lads in the county of Durham. kApplause). They were often told that wages were regulated by the law of supply' and demand, but could they tell him of one Single case in which wages had followed the market when it is rising without an effort of t the workmen to push them up. (gear, Hear). He claimed that though Unions could not fix wages in some instances they could in others. They could fix wages according to the price of the produce of labour, and that was all they asked to do. They said further that Unions could keep up wages longer than they would otherwise be kept up and they could force them up sooner. (Ap- plause.) Again referring to the improved condition of work-men, Mr. Wilson said, emoting from Mnlhall's statistics, that there were in 1887 and every year follow- ing 1,000 lives of miners Raved in comparsion with the rate of mortality prevailing at the time the Queen com- menced to reign. What had brought that about was the very close scrutiny that followed in the coroners' courts on the heels of every calamity. Twenty or thirty years ago when a calamity took place there was a convenient sort of stereotyped verdict—they died an accidental death. At that time there were no combinations, but now when an accident happened there were men who volunteered to go downthe mine, and after the saving of life was over, these men made it their peculiar duty to endeavour to trace out the source of the explosion, not for the purpose of punishing but for the purpose of prevention. Skilful lawyers were also employed and they followed the course of the evidence, and when the cause of the disaster was found, they demanded that in future greater' care should be taken to guard against the recurrence of the calamity. (Hear, hear.) One of the great benefits of a Trades Union was to place workmen on a par with their em- ployers. A power which took a workman out of a posi- tion of dependence upon the will of an employer, and which placed him directly, or indirectly through his chosen representatives, on an equal with his employer, was a power that ought to be maintained at all risks and all costs. One of the primary objects of a Trades Union should be the procuring of better wages, and especially for the lowest class of labour. There was a selfish reason for that, because, so long as there was hanging upon the frinee of skilled labour a large body of unskilled labour, it was a source of the greatest danger to themselves. (Hear, hear.) The progress of the working classes will never be so speedy as it should be were those lower down in the strata in better cimunistances than they are. He therefore appealed to the skilled workmen to consider the relations of this lower class of labour to themselves. The speaker then referred in gratified terms to the many dif- ferent classes of labourers represented at the Trades Con- gress this year, a Congress at which 700,000 more workmen were represented than at the previous congress, and in conclusion he made an eloquent appeal to those present to join their trade societies and foe trade societies to federate. Mr. W. RIILLOCK, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Wilson and Mr. Jamieson, mentioned that the tanners of Warrington had recently formed a union which now numbered something like 200 members. Mr. T. HOUGHTON seconded the pmposition,which was carried by acclammation, and Mr. JAMIESON responded. Mr. T. MALKIN moved, and Mr. T. RIOTS'S seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and this having been accorded and responded to, the meeting terminated.

ST. PAUL'S CHOIR TRIP. The senior members of St. Paul's choir held their annual excursion on Monday, the place selected be- ing Windermere. An early start was made, and after a pleasant journey the lake was reached at about 8.30. Breakfast over the party proceeded to the ferry and sailed up the lake to Ambleside, and afterwards proceeded to the beautiful village of Grasmere. The church and Wordsworth's grave were duly visited, the lovely scenery of the neigh- bourhood being much admired. At five o'clock the excursionists returned to Windermere, where a sub- stantial knife and fork tea was much enjoyed. The Vicar addressed a few words to the choir, and thanked them and their excellent organist for their earnest work during the past year. A start for home was made at 6.55, Warrington being safely reached at 11.30.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT MOORE.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT MOORE.

- - An interesting presentation took place at the Wesleyan School, Moore, on Monday evening, when Mrs. Jackson, the wife of the Rev. E. 11. Jackson, was the recipient of a handsome wedding gift from the members of the Wesleyan congregation wor- shipping in that village. After the subscribers had partaken of tea, provided by Mrs. Cartwright, a tasteful salad bowl of silver-mounted Worcester china, with servers and table rests, and an elegant sterling silver scent bottle with suitable inscription and fitted into morocco case, were presented to Mrs. Jackson, with the hearty good wishes of all the Wesleyan friends. Several speeches alluding with affectionate appreciation to Mrs. Jackson's work in connection with the chapel and schools were delivered, and many grateful allusions were made to the ministry of the Rev. E. H. Jackson. his work having been carried on in so kindly and acceptable a manner. Afterwards, the latter, in a happy speech, returned thanks on behalf of his wife, and the proceedings terminated with prayer. THE BIRTH AND DEATH HATE OF WARRINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, August 30th, 1890.—The mean temperature was 51.6 Fahrenheit, and therefore 44 degrees colder than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature, 64 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 29th inst, and the minimum temperature, 33 Fahrenheit, on the 30th inst. The rainfall measured 1 in. The general direction of the wind was Westerly. During the week, which was the 35th of the current year, 26 births and 15 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 15.6 per thousand, against 21.32, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 25.8 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 4 from diarrhcea, 1 from abscess, 1 from cancer,' 1 from phthisis, 1 from old age, 2 from brain disease, 2 from lung disease, 1 from heart disease, 1 from liver disease. One ease of scarlatina was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.--JoHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
