ALLEGED MEAT POISONING AT CROFT. On Saturday, at the Newton Petty Sessions, a Croft farmer named William Southern, was sum- , moned for unlawfully placing, or causing to be placed upon land, certain meat mixed or saturated with poison to such an• extent as to be calculated to destroy life. Mi. W. H. Jenkins, of Warrington, prosecuted, and Mr. T. Swift, barrister (Liverpool), instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles, defended. Mr. Jenkins stated that on Sunday, the 29th June, Miss Elizabeth Makin, cook in the employ of the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, vicar of Croft, took out a valuable collie dog, belonging to the son of tlie vicar. The dog was muzzled, and ran into one of the fields near the rectory. On returning to Miss Makin the dog seemed to have a yellow substance about its mouth, and appeared to be very listless and sleepy. On the following morning the animal was found dead in its kennel. A post-mortem examination of the body was made by Mr. Darwall, veterinary surgeon. Leigh, and a portion of the contents of the stomach were examined by Mr. Ruddock, analytical chemist at Whitecross Wire Works, Warrington. The result was that traces of poison in the shape of morphine were found. Evidence was given in corroboration of Mr.Jenkins' statement,and to the effect thatpieces of meat had been previously seen in defendant's possession, and it was alleged that defendant had stated to a neighbouring farmer that the meat was poisoned. The dog was said to be a valuable one, and Mr. Kirkman, jun., deposed that it was worth .£2O or .£3O. For the defence, Mr. Swift contended that there was no evidence that the defendant had laid, or caused to be laid, any poison; and that there was not the slightest tittle of evidence that he possessed, or purchased, or ever had any Thor- -1 phine in his possession. He also submitted that the information was ba3, and the particular offence ' was not specified. After a lengthy hearing, the Bench dismissed the case for want of sufficient evi- dence. - -
ST. MAIM'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, BUTTERDUUSET- -- --
STEMMT.

Sunday last was the thirteenth anniversary of the opening of this church, the building being opened August 31st, 1877, when the present Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. O'Reilly) celebrated pontifical High Mass in the presence of a representative congrega- tion of the leading inhabitants of the town of all denominations. The celebrated Mgr. Capel preached in the opening sermons, morning and evening, and many who listened to the eloquent Monsignor have since been called from amongst us. The church is built from a design of the great Gothic architect, the late Mr. Welby Pugin, and the additions in the interior are designed by Mr. Pugin's successor, Messrs. Pugin & Pugin, Westminster. The building is 150 ft. long and 52ft. wide, and rises to a height of 75ft. The interior is acknowledged by many com- petent judges of church architecture to be equal to i f not to surpass any church in Lancashire for beauty of line and graceful proportions. The reat channel arch rises to the roof of the church, and is one of the principal features of the interior. When opened the church was far from complete, but many additions have been made since. The hard-working Superior, Father Sumner, is to be congratulated upon the work which has been done during the last few years. The work in hand at the present time; cost- ing several hundred pounds, is the erection of an altar to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and stone screens tor the chancel and a small stained window over the altar. Messrs. Boulton and Co. are now carving the altar and screens, which are expected to be in position during October. The painted window will represent the five wounds of the Saviour. The church stands upon freehold ground, and the shop tenanted by Mr. Stirrup belongs to the church. At some future time this shop will be taken down to give a better approach and entrance to the building. The old infirmary, now used as the Inland Revenue Offices, also belongs to the church. CRITOHLEVB Tailoring meets the times.—Advt.

TRAVELLING WITHOUT TICKET. Yesterday, at the Warrington Occasional Court, a man named Andrew Malcolmson was charged with travelling between Edgehill and Newton, without having paid his fare. He was remanded to the next Newton Petty Sessions.

ANOTHER OUTBREAR OF SWINE FiNvzlt. An outbreak of swine fever has been discovered on the premises of Mr. Joseph Ilorrocks, provision dealer, 52 School-brow. One pig was found dead in the stye, and Mr. Shawcross, borough veterinary surgeon,certified that it had died from swine fever.

THE COMING linvisiox. As previous3y announced in our columns, Mr. T. T. Foard, revising barrister, will on Monday next commence the revision of the voter's list for War- rington. The sittings will be held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall. It is expected that the work will be of a routine character. WYCI.SFFE• CHURCH Cucum. On Saturday the members of this choir enjoyed , their annual excursion, under the hospitable leader- ship of Mr. and Mrs. Armitage. The place of resort was Norbury, Cheshire, and a very pleasant time was spent. The weather was fine and bright, no rain descending until l the return journey had been made. THE SUDDEN DEATH AT DAN WAVY STATION. The Coroner (Mr. Brighouse) has- decided not to hold an inquest regarding the death of Mr. Thomas Metcalfe, of Bradford, who died 'suddenly on the platform at Bank Quay railway station+ yesterday afternoon week. The matter has been referred to the registrar, who has certified as to the cause of death.

RECREATIVE EVENING SCHOOLS ASSOCTACION. In pursuance of one of its principal objects, that of establishing evening schools and. classes this Association has arranged for science classes in con- nection with the department of Science .and Art of the Committee of Council on Education. The classes will be opened on the 18th September,. and the teacher will be Mr. B. Davies, off Newton-le-Willows. It will be seen from particulars given in our adver- tising columns that other classes are also being ar- ranged by the Association. SUDDEN DEATH OF A, BAKER. Yesterday afternoon, at the bridewell, W..T. Husband held an inquest on view, of the body of Richard Lee (34), who bad been living in lodgings at Peasley Cross, St. Helens, but who died on Wed- nesday morning at the residence of his mother, at Gas-st., Warrington. The deceased; who was a baker, caught a severe cold about a, fortnight ego and at his request was brought to Warrington last Tuesday. He was then very ill, and died next morning. After hearing the evidence the jury found that death resulted from natural causes, resulting from taking a cold. MUSIC IN THE PARE:

The band of the Gas Engineers (employ6s of Messrs. T. Fletcher and Co.), will play the following selection of music in the Park, on Sunday afternoon, commencing at three o'clock. Conductor, Mr. W. Waterfield. Grand slow march " Honour to the Brave:"....Riviere. Overture " Semiramide." Rossini-, (By desire.) Clarionet solo "Austrian Hymn." Haydn.. (Solo clarionet, Mr. W. Kirk.) Chorus "Glory to God." liandd. (From the "Messiah.") Overture "William Tell." Rossini- " God Savo the Queen.' INTERESTING EXHIBITION OF ANIMALS' IN BRIDGE-ST. There is quite an extensive collection of animals- = view at Mr. Hodgkinson's establishment in Bridge-st. It is on a large scale, the whole of the extensive frontage being devoted to the purpose, and is in connection with the magnificient display of furs of every kind which the firm are making; a speciality of. This shows a commendable spirit of enterprise amongst local tradesmen, who can only by keeping abreast of the times keep trade at home, and thus benefit the town. The exhibition includes all kinds of animals whose furs are such as to represent the stock inside, and it is of such a character that crowds gather in front of the shop,. especially in the evenings, to have a look at it. GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD. The first meeting of the newly-elected Board was held on Thursday afternoon. There were present the Rev. E. S. Jackson, Captain Ridgway, and Messrs. W. P. Skelton, John Cook, and S. Sutton (clerk.). The Clerk presided pro tern and read a'communication from the Education Department stating that the above-named gentlemen had been elected • to the Board. On the motion of the Rev. E. S. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Skelton, Captain Ridgway was re- elected chairman of the Board for the next three years. On the motion of the Rev.. E. S. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Cook, Mr. Skelton was re-appointed vice-chairman.—There being one vacancy on the Board it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Cook, seconded by Mr. Skelton, that Mr. Joseph Wright, of Chapel Farm, Great Sankey, be elected a member of the Board.—This was the principal business. UNJUST WEIGHTS. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Rebecca Locker, greengrocer, Warrington, was sum- moned for having weights that were unjust, on the 15th August, at Newton. The case was proved by Superintendent Weir, who stated that on Friday, the 15th ult., he was in Crow-lane, Newton, when. he saw a horse and greengrocer's cart, belonging to the defendant. He took possession of the weights, and on trying them found that one, a four-pound weight, was 11 drachms light, and that another, a half-pound weight, was 7 drachms light.. A person in the employ of the defendant. appeared to say that the offence was caused without the knowledge of Mrs. Locker, hut, the Bench considered the case was proved, and imposed a fine of 20s. and costs. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Broadhurst, grocer, Winwick- road, was summoned for a similar offence and fined 10s. and costs; Edward key, fiShmonger,.Winwick- road, was fined ss. and costs; and George Solbery, off-license holder, Winwick-road, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. The defence in each case was that there had been no intention of having light weights. DRUIDS' MEETING. The annual meeting of the Widow and Orphans Fund of the Warrington District Society of Druids was held at the Rose and Crown Inn,. Bridge-st., when there were present the Trustees, P.D.G.M Geo. Roughley, P.D.G.M. George. Jolley, and P.R.A. James Spencer; president, William, Ilankey, and vice-president, P.N.G.A. Samuel Caldwell ; also the secretary,P.D.G.M.John Booth; storekeener P.D.G.M. William Bibby, and the delegates, P.TIG.M. James Wilcock, P.D.G.M. Peter Langley, P:D.O.M. Samuel Dunbobin, P.R.A. James Simcock,P.A. Robert Pardue, P.R.A. Charles Rigby, P.A. James Booth, P.A. Charles Peover, P.A. Charles Cooper, MGM. William Cross- -1,11, P.A. James Booth' P.A. Henry Glover, P.D.G.M. Edward Pointon, P.A. George Spencer. The balance sheet was read,showing the total worth of the funds to be as follows :—General fund, £632 Os. 2d.•' man- agement fund, ..£35 7s. 4d. ; crockery fund .E 35 16s. ;by cash in corporation invested, £400; by cash in savings bank, £342 138. 6d.; by cash in treasurer's hands, £lO ss. lid. An increase was shown on the present year's working of £23 4.1'1d, After a convivial evening had been spent the follow- ing officers were duly elected :: President, P.N.G.A. Samuel Caldwell; vice-president, P.N.G.A. George Spencer; the trustees, treasurer and secretary were re-appointed; auditors for the year, D.G.M. Wm. Croskill, D.C.S. Thomas Roberts. This fund pays the school fees of all deceased members' childreng in need of it. C VITCIILET. Practical Tailor. Bold-st..tWarrington.—Advt. THE WARRINGTON WoRKINGMEN'S OPEN An TOTAL ABSTINENCE MISSION. On Sunday the usual meetings were held on the enclosed ground off Bevesey-st. In the afternoon Mr. E. Robertson, the secretary, presided, and the following addressed the meeting: Messrs. W. Rig- ginson, J. F. Owen, and J. Drury. In the evening' Mr. E. Robertson was again in the chair, and 1%1 essrs. J. 0. Reilly, J. Owen, C. H. Mills, and J. Drury gave very encouraging addresses. Another meeting was held at Bridge Foot. Mr. T. Frain (vice-president) presided, and Messrs. J. 0. Reilly and J. Kilduff spoke. Sankey's solos were sung by the choir. Several persons took the pledge. The meetings were well attended. On Mcnda3: the above society held its first half yearly meeting, at the Cocoa rooms, Horsemarket-street. Mr. J. Drury (President) presided, and the reports of the officers were taken. Mr. R. Robertson, the secretary, report- ed that there was a membership of 66 members making an increase since July of 26: He also report- ed the outdoor work to 'be a great success, they hav- ing taken over 75 pledges since May last. Mr. Rob- inson, financial secretary, and Mr. J. Drury. Trees,, also gave their reports, showing that there was a small balance in hand. All the reports 'Wore re- ceived as very satisfactory. The officers and Ex- cutive were elected for the next six months, those elected being : President,Mr. J. Price ; vice-presicl-; eat, Mr. C. H.Mills; secretary, Mr. E. Robertson trt asurer, Mr. Drury ; finance secretary. Mr. C. Rob- inson ; assistant secretary, Mr. G. Perklow. There were over 40 members pre.soit.

TRII' TO LLANGOLLEN. On Tuesday about thirty members of' the Warring- ton Bakers' Association had a very enjoyable trip to Llangollen. Arrived there, they journeyed by boat to the Horse Shoe Waterfalls, and aftervrctrds en- joyed a capital dinner at the Ponsonby Arms. Dinner over, the party separated, some going to Corwen, and others to the Oid ,Castle. Mr. Strange was chairman of the Committee, and Mr. Davies secretary.

div.head: WATCH COMMITTEE AND THE
div.p: THE WATCH COMMITTEE AND THE
POLICE.

On Thursday an ordinary meetnig of the Watch Committee of the Corporation was, held, Alderman Harrison presiding in the absence of the Mayor, who is chairman of the Committee.. The matters I dinussed at Tuesday's Town Counuil meeting in regard to the police force were mentioned in an informal way, but no further action wne taken in regard to them.. We are informed that the Com- mittee will adhere to the decision promoting Con- stable Francis Jones to be sergeant.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSERMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSERMENT COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this Committee-was-held , at the Workhouse, on Friday. The Rev: G. F. , Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. It. Heaton and John Houghton ; S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and W. Owen (valuer). ALLEGED BOTCOTTIrt44 N4HAA WARRINGTON.—Tat W. Robinson appealed against the assessment of his land' and osier beds off Manchester-road. The reasons given for the appeal were in effect that the appellant had besertur- able to make a protitableuse of the land. He said that during the last three years he had had to burn the crops' on the land • and his averageretarns for the last fifteen years bad left nothing forrent.—The Clerk said he sup- , posed the land was as good as other land in the same. neighbourhood.—Mr. Robinson: Yes.—The Clerk: Then it should be assessed on the same lines.—Mr. Houghton : Why don't you get the crops. off the land like other farmers ?—Mr. Robinson r We cut it three years and could not sell ; I have some hay there four years old.-- Mr. Heaton: What do you, do,with your osier beds ? Mr. Robinson: They have been three years uncut because I could not sell them.—The Chairman explained that those were matters the Committee had nothingi to do with; they could only assess the land at its proper value. Mr. Owen would, therefore, take the matter in hand.—Mr. Robinson said he had not had a shilling of rent from his land for fifteen years, and the sole cause of this.; was the boycott that was organised against him. The property was in the hands of solicitors to let, but they had never had any offer.—Mr. W. Houghton asked if somebody had not offered to cut the crops for him.—lr. Robinson said a person had offered to do so on condition that he got the crop. He (Mr. Robinson) said there was a good many . cheeky people in this country, and that person was one 'a them. (Laughter.) He went on to complain of the alleged boycott of his property, and' was reading from a newspaper cutting when the Chairman again interrupted by saying the matter would be placed in Mr. Owen's hands.—Mr. Robinson : I have done my duty to England, but England has not doneitsclouty to me.—The Chairman said they could not do with that any longer. '—Mr. Robinson said he was boycotted bv a system, and he should try to put it on the right shoulders. He was 'offering a reward of £loo.—Mr. Heaton 7 The best plan for you is to go home and let this land.—Mr. Robinson : It is very easy to say so, but they leading lawyers in Warrington cannot let it. Mine is a• worse case of boy- cott than any in Ireland.—The Chairman said they were sorry for him but they could only deal with the matter in ,the usual way.—Mr. Robinson said he did not want any- body's pity, but he should show up the-blessed parasites. (Laughter.)—Mr. Robinson then retired, from the room. VALUER 'S REPORT.—The Valuer reported that since the last meeting he had made the following valuations : Mr. Joseph Glover, Penketh, house, gross- £ll, rateable £9 10s., workshops gross £2 10s., rateable £2; Mr. John Ansdell, house, Penketh, gross £lBi.rateable £l5 ss. ; M. The latter had shown them that all receipt's for adverbs- ments had been included in the accounts which were submitted when the assessment on therailway was fixed, and it was recommended therefore that/ tihe assessment for advertisements be taken off. Messrs.. Sullivan and Co., ,chemical works. div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

TRIP TO FRODSILAIL On Wednesday several junior classee of girls in connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School went to Frodsham for a trip. The party,. numbering about 2.04,. under the leadership of Miss 11, Routledge, left Warrington for Frodsham about. 2'.! o'clock, and the latter place was reached without any mishaps. After-a ramble on the hills, tea was partaken of in a hearty manner. Later in the evening the home journey was commenced, Penketh. being reached shortly alter nine, everyone having, spent a very enjoyable day. IWES-LITTAN MUTUAL hIPROVEN ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening a meeting,of the members off the above association was held to, complete the election of officers, and to arrange the syllabus for the,. cowing season. The President (Mr. J. T. Gomersall) having resigned, Mr. (3.. R. Parker pro- posed that Mr. T. Gandy be elected to take his place.. Mr. Watson seconded, and the proposition was carried unanimously. Mr. Philip Hughes was eleeten assistant secretary. There was some die- , mission as to the advisability of Changing the even- ing of meeting, but as no more convenient evening could be found, the matter was left as before. After thisthe secretary presented a draft of the syllabus, which, after a few alterations,,waa adopted. The mooting closed with singing and pryer. ESSAY ON " VEGRTALLR. TOOD." Last evening week at the meeting of the Youngj Men's Christian Association, .Mr. A.. Tucker read an. essay, entitled " Vegetable FOod.'_" There was good attendance of members. He dealt first with, the chemical combination of different vegetables,. and then followed on with. statistics showing the extent of the cultivation and consumption of cere- als. Ile described the various roots used as food, and compared their respectiVenntritive properties. He said that good wholesome food and temperate habits were the best means of ensuring health. ie essay, which was given in, a very attractive and interesting manner, was attentively listened to,,and at the close a vote of thanks was accorded to , 3lr. r Tucker.

A DELIGHTFUL FLAYoun, Cameron's Areca-Nut Tooth Paste ; by using this delicious Aromatic Dentifrice. the Enamel of the Teeth becomes white, sound, and polished like Ivory. It is exceedingly fragrant.—Advt. A London news agency says the date for the aorma- tion of the proposed Chemical Union has been :farther postponed until November. A coroner's jury, on Thursday, found a verdict of "Wilful murder" against John Wise, who shot Mrs. Davies, mother of the man who eloped with Ilia, wife at Deepfields, Sedgley.. The juey added a mitigating rider. The steamer Volturno arrived at Cardiff a hew days ago with a non-union crew-, who have since their arrival been guarded by police On Thursday moroing, they quarrelled among themselves, and a sailor named Fred Graves was seriously stabbed. His alleged; assailant, John Ilannes, was arrested. At the Bolton Police Cone, on Thursday morning Jane Dwyer was fined 40s, and costs, for cruelly ill-treating and starving a child, named Therese Barron which she had taken out of the workhouse to keep. The child was bruised about the body, Igs, and head,and' weighed only 29A1b., being hlb. less than it ought to have weighc The child was insured. THE PREMIER AFTER HIS COSTS. A Dublin corms, pondent says that Mr. and Mrs. O'Brien, and Mr. Dillon arrived io that city from Thurles on Wednesday nigh.. Mr. O'Brien was served in the railway carriage, on be- half of Loed Salisbury, with a notice toshow cause why he should sot pay in,600 costs of the; proceedings indtis action against the Premier. The EAsteddfod Was continued at Bangor on 'Thurs- day, and during the day the Queett of Roumania, Vra3 one of the visitors. Sir John Putesteta read an address of weltome; in which complimentary reference was: made to her Majesty's literary gifts. The ceremony oh chair- ing the bard, who this year is Tudno, otherwise the Rev. T. 0. Jones, was performed daring the day. The strain of the Australian strike is being severely I felt in l..ondon by shippers, shipowners, and afore than , all by stevedores. The present is usually the busiest part of the year in the colonial export trade, and all the berths in the South, West, and East India Docks are generally taken up. Now, however, many- berths are ; vacant, and the export sheds are empty. This naturally, . means less employment fordockers and stevedores.

_ Mrs. Yerburgh, wife of Mr. Yerburgh, M.P. for Ches- ter, and daughter of the late Mr. Daniel Thwaites, mem- ber' for Blackburn, has just contributed £l,OOO to the funds of the Blackburn Ragged School. div.head: HARVEST OUTLOOK IN _DONEGAL:
div.p: THE HARVEST OUTLOOK IN _DONEGAL:

The rain which has continually fallen for the last fortnight has intensified the expectation of distress throughout Donegal from the failure of the potatoe crop. General Sankey, chairman of the Board of Works, and Mr. Jackson, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, are now in Donegal inspecting the light railway routes and inspiring into the necessity for relief works.

TARRING AN UNPOPULAR OFFICER. Itt,is reported in Cork that, as the result of a complaint to the War-office, an officer of the 2ad Battalion Welsh Regiment, stationed there, had been taken out of bed and tarred by his fidlow-officers, with whom he had strained relations. Two officers have been dismissed, and three others removed to other regiments. Although the military refused information the report is believed to be correct.

FRODSHAM AND HELSBY DRAINAta BOARD. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a GENERAL MEETING of the Ratepayers within the district of the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board will be held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday the twelfth day of Septem- ber, 1890, at seven o'clock in the evening for the purpose of electing new members of the Board. The number of mem- bers to be elected 13 15 and the qualifications are as follows The proprietor of not less than 20 statute acres within the district, The heir apparent of the proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the district. The occupier yearly or otherwise of not less than 30 statute acres within the district. The agent of a proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the district such agent acting under a written appointment. HENRY BESWICK, Returning Officer. Frodsham, 3rd September, 1890.

REUBEN PEARSON, AFTER more than 25 years' experience in the treatment of disease, is pleased to be able to commend to the public the testimony, voluntarily offered by Many of his past patients. In cases of Rheumatism, Gant, Sciatica and Lumbago, his Massage and other treatment has proved marvellously success- ful. For some years past he has made this treatment a spe- cial feature and study, and iii the cases he has had under the sanction and supervision af Medical men, he has produced re- sults which even they admit have been singular and excep- tional. "REUBEN'S HYDRO," Rock Cottages, Greenfield, October 6th. DEAR SIR, It is with no small feeling of gratitude to you and for the good of humanity in general that I write to you, and you are at liberty to make such use of this testimonial as you think proper. I was under the treatment of several doctors where I live, for Sciatica, but to no use. I was then sent to Buxton for a time. I received no relief under their treatment, and I was then told by the doctors that they could do nothing for me and that I should never again be able to walk straight, I felt this to be very poor consolation and had naturally a great desire to recover, then the doctor advised me to go into the Manchester Infirmary. I was there fifteen weeks and had a good kind doctor, but I got worse every week until I could not walk. I went through the most agonising pain that ever man could go through. I was blistered and burned with hot needles having them put in my leg and the electric battery was played on them whilst they were in. I thought they were trying me for a soldier to see if I could stand steel ; but thanks to providence you came to my relief. You know the situation I was left in, but you did not go by on tke other side, but acted the part of the Good Samaritan. for which I thank God, for in nine weeks under your treatment I could move about to the no small astonishment of my neighbours, for none ever thought. I believe, to see me walk straight again, and my doctor stated that he could not believe It was me when he saw me. And, Sir, through the blessing of God through your treatment I enjoy whetter atatis of health, than I have done for a long time before, and for your kind treatment to MO May Heaven smile upon you and yours. I remain yours, AMBROSE SCHOFIELD. ILITMEN'I HYDRO', AITRINCEM.M. EXTRA CHARGE AFTER 8 P.M.

CASE OF ALLEGED WRONGFUL CON- VICTION IN DERBYSHIRE. The Bentley Carr poaching case, which attracted 3, good deal of attention some months since on account 0' alleged wrongful convictions, has ended in the release of the prisoners. Four men were convicted at the DerbY Assizes nearly a year since for a murderous assault on 3 policeman, and were each sentenced to five years' per servitude. Doubts were afterwards thrown uPon Lb! case, and four other men were arrested and tried for wv same'offence, but were discharged. The Home Seeret-arY' after exhaustive inquiries into the matter, has now ordered the release of the convicted men, and they ha" ' just returned to their homes near Ashbourne. LORD HARTINGTON ON LIBERAL UNIONISM. Speaking at York on Wednesday night, Lord Harting" ton said the Liberal Unionists had been likened to vvolvee in sheeps clothing,but he thought the metaphor ill-chosen. Rather were they the watch-dogs striving to protect ths peaceful flocks committed to their charge. One b°ll Lnited the Unionists, and that was a firm detertninatiot to resist revolution whether it showed its head in Ireland or elsewhere, and at the same time to extend to as to other parts of the Queen's dominion, every measur,3 of justice and conciliation that reason could deman?'• Great progress had, he maintained, been made 111 strengthening the Unionist organisation, and in man); constituencies there was a percentage of Liberal elector who, while they remained Liberal, still continued to 173 Unionists. He did not pretend that it was a large Pef. _ centage, but it was one which where constituencies vt,e,t°' pretty evenly balanced would be sufficient to turn Pt' scale. • The Parnellite party had carried on a cam Par, in Ireland founded upon discontent and greed. But believed their most formidable method of gaining their ends had been the campaign in the House of Common. against the credit and dignity of Parliament. They had o succeeded in coercing, if not in convincing, one nr f greatest political parties in the State in the direction 0 Home Rule.

ALLEGED Dearaoe.--John White was summoned for damaging a paddock belonging to William Stringer, on the 30th ult. The case was dismissed. NEGLIGENT AeragsricEs.--Alice Bibby was summoned to show cause why she should not be committed to prison for disobeying an order of the:magistrates to filifti her contract as an apprentice to John Bolton. The case was adjourned for a month to see if she would return to work.—Annie Cunningham was summoned by Edwin Mills on a similar charge. She was sent to prison for seven days. -- WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. James Tinsley. DRUNKENNESS.—Herbert Wilson and Richard Bilston were charged with being drunk at Rixton on the previ- ous night, and were each fined ss. and costs, the alterna- tive being seven days' imprisonment. WARRINGTON COUNTY PETIT SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington and Mr. J. Tinsley. DRUNKENNESS.—James Coyne for having been drunk at Penketh, on the 23rd ult., was fined ss. and costs.— Thomas Arstall, for having been drunk and disorderly on the 17th ult., at Rixton, was fined ss. and costs —George Arstall, for a similar offence committed at Rixton, on the 17th ult., was also fined ss. and costs. THE Dom ORDER.--Samuel Kfishall summoned for allowing a dog to be at large unmuzzled, was fined is. and costs. SLEEPY DRITERS.—WiIIiam Jackson was fined ss. and costs for being asleep while in charge of a horse and cart at Penketh.—Samuel Walker, summoned for committing a similar offence at Poulton, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell jun., and Mr. H. Wade-Deacon. DRUNEENNESS.—For this offence John Cavanagh, Geo. Simpson, Richard Leatherbarrow, Samuel Pope, and John Rowan, were each fined S. and costs. Owen Tansey was fined 10s. and costs. INDEcENT BEHAVIOUR.—WiIIiam Marshall, of no fixed abode, was charged with behaving in an indecent manner on some waste ground in Cross-st.. on Saturday. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to two months' hard labour. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell and W. L. M'Clure. DRUNICKNNESS.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon John Walsh, John Fowler, Charles Lee, Sarah Maher, and John Spencer.—Sarah Jervis was fined 10s. and costs and Jane Drury, an old offender, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. ScgooL BOARD CasEs.—A number of parents were sum- moned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of S. was imposed in each case. DAMAGE TO A DOOR.—William Shields and George Simpson, were summoned for doing wilful damage to the door of the house of Mary Walsh. At a quarter to twelve on Sunday night the defendants called at the complainant's house for a bottle of ginger beer. They were under the influence of drink, and smashed six glasses and broke one panel of the door. The defend- ants called two companions, who declared they broke the panel in trying to burst the door open.—The defend- ants were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs and ordered to pay the damage. RUNCORN PETrY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele. TRANSFER—The license of the Camden Hotel, Surrey- at., was transferred from Wm. Walkey to Wm. C. Mason. STREET OnsTaticrzoN.— Mendel Blank, furniture dealer,'Bridge-st., was summoned for obstructing the footpath by placing furniture in front of his shop. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, who defended, sailthefurniture was not there any length of time and waeplaced there previous to being carried into the shop.—A fine of 6d. and costs Bs. 6d., was imposed. AssauLT.—Ralph Done, was charged with assaulting Richard Rhodes at Weston. The men had ' some words" about the changing of half a sovereign and the defend- ant struck Rhodes on the chest. Fined ss. and costs 10s. NEGLECTING BIS WlFE.—Mosea Pierce, stone getter, was summoned by Mary, his wife, for neglecting to sup- port her. The woman said the defendant left her three months ago and had not since contributed toiler support. He was earning over 30s. per week.—The defendant con- tended that he only received 18s. to 20s. per week.—The plaintiff asked for an order for 15s. per week, and the Bench made the order accordingly. DRUNlC.—Edward M'Cormick, Joseph Mellor, Michael Hogan, Elizabeth Cross, and John Ryan, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—Andrew Connell, a youth, was charged with stealing a quantity of sweets belonging to James Naylor, confectioner &c., of Warrington.—As the prosecutor did not appear, the prisoner was discharged.
